`Read(./secrets/**)`
`Bash(cat secrets)`
`Read(./secrets)`
objective.explanation: Read and Edit rules use gitignore-style patterns. `**` matches files at any depth, while `*` matches only one level. `./secrets` on its own targets just that path, and a Bash rule does not control Claude's Read tool.

subjective.question: What is plan mode in Claude Code, and when would you use it?
subjective.answer: Plan mode is a read-only permission mode. Claude can read files, search the codebase and think through the problem, but it cannot edit files or run state-changing commands until I approve its plan. I enter it with Shift+Tab, which cycles default, auto-accept edits and plan, or I start with `claude --permission-mode plan`. I use it for larger changes: a feature touching several files, a refactor, or work in a part of the codebase I do not know well. It separates thinking from doing. I see Claude's understanding of the problem before any code changes, so I can correct wrong assumptions cheaply. For a one-line fix or a typo, plan mode is overhead and I skip it.
keyPoints: Read-only: no edits or state-changing commands until approval
Entered via Shift+Tab cycle or `--permission-mode plan`
Best for multi-file features, refactors, unfamiliar code
Catches wrong assumptions before code is written
Skip it for trivial changes

subjective.question: Claude has produced a plan for your feature. How do you review it before approving edits?
subjective.answer: I read the plan as if it were a design review from a junior colleague. First, does it understand the goal correctly, including edge cases? Second, which files will it touch? If it plans to change files I did not expect, such as a shared utility or config, I ask why. Third, does it follow existing patterns in the codebase rather than inventing new ones? Fourth, does it include tests and say how it will verify the change? Fifth, is the scope right, with no extra 'improvements' I did not ask for? If anything is off, I stay in plan mode and give feedback, for example 'reuse the existing validator in utils/validate.ts'. I approve only when the plan is specific enough that I could predict the diff.
keyPoints: Check understanding of the goal and edge cases
Check which files will change and why
Check it follows existing codebase patterns
Check tests and a verification step are included
Iterate in plan mode before approving; watch for scope creep

subjective.question: Explain the 'explore, plan, code, commit' workflow and why each step matters.
subjective.answer: It is a four-step loop for non-trivial work. Explore: Claude reads the relevant files, often in plan mode or with an instruction not to write code yet. This builds the context it needs. Plan: Claude proposes a concrete approach, and I review and refine it. This is where mistakes are cheapest to fix. Code: after I approve, Claude implements the plan and checks its work by running tests or the linter. Commit: Claude writes a clear commit message and, if needed, opens a pull request, after I have reviewed the diff. The value is that Claude does not jump straight into coding. Without the explore and plan steps, it may solve the wrong problem or ignore existing patterns. The commit step keeps changes small and reversible.
keyPoints: Explore: read relevant code first, no edits
Plan: concrete approach reviewed by the developer
Code: implement and verify with tests
Commit: reviewed diff, clear message, small reversible change
Prevents jumping to code on the wrong problem

subjective.question: Compare the main permission modes in Claude Code: default, acceptEdits, plan and bypassPermissions.
subjective.answer: Default mode asks for permission the first time Claude wants to use each tool, such as editing a file or running a shell command, unless an allow rule already covers it. acceptEdits, or auto-accept edits, lets Claude edit files without asking, but it still asks before running commands not on the allow-list. I use it when I trust the plan and want speed. Plan mode is read-only: Claude researches and proposes a plan, and nothing changes until I approve. bypassPermissions, started with `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, skips all prompts. It is only safe in an isolated container or VM with no sensitive access, because Claude can then run any command. In the terminal, Shift+Tab cycles default, auto-accept edits and plan.
keyPoints: Default: prompt on first use of each tool
acceptEdits: file edits auto-approved, commands still checked
Plan: read-only until plan approved
bypassPermissions: no prompts, isolated environments only
Shift+Tab cycles default → accept edits → plan

subjective.question: How do allow, ask and deny permission rules work, and what happens when they conflict?
subjective.answer: Permission rules live under `permissions` in settings.json. Allow rules let Claude use a tool without prompting, for example `Bash(npm run test:*)`. Ask rules force a confirmation prompt even if something else would allow it, which is useful for risky commands like `git push`. Deny rules block a tool entirely, for example `Read(./.env)` to protect secrets. When rules match the same action, deny wins over ask, and ask wins over allow. So if I allow broad reading of the project but deny `Read(./.env)`, the env file stays blocked. This lets me write generous allow-lists for speed and still keep a hard safety net. The `:*` suffix in Bash rules is a prefix match, so I write rules carefully to avoid allowing more than intended.
keyPoints: Allow: no prompt; ask: always confirm; deny: blocked
Conflict order: deny beats ask beats allow
Use deny for secrets like `Read(./.env)`
`Bash(cmd:*)` is a prefix match
Broad allows plus narrow denies give speed and safety

subjective.question: Describe the settings file scopes in Claude Code and their order of precedence. Which file would you commit?
subjective.answer: From highest to lowest precedence: enterprise managed settings, then command-line arguments, then `.claude/settings.local.json`, then `.claude/settings.json`, then the user file `~/.claude/settings.json`. Managed settings are set by an organisation and cannot be overridden, which suits security policy. CLI arguments apply to one launch. The local project file is for my personal rules in this repo and is git-ignored. The shared project file is committed to git, so the whole team gets the same allow and deny rules, such as allowing the test command and denying `.env` reads. The user file holds my personal defaults for every project. I commit `.claude/settings.json` only, and I keep personal experiments in the local file so I do not push my preferences onto the team.
keyPoints: Order: managed → CLI → local project → shared project → user
Managed settings cannot be overridden
Commit `.claude/settings.json` for team rules
`.claude/settings.local.json` is personal and git-ignored
`~/.claude/settings.json` holds personal defaults across projects

subjective.question: Write a project permissions block for a Node.js app so Claude can run tests and lint without prompts, must confirm before pushing, and can never read env files. Explain your choices.
subjective.answer: In `.claude/settings.json` I would write: `{"permissions": {"allow": ["Bash(npm run test:*)", "Bash(npm run lint)"], "ask": ["Bash(git push:*)"], "deny": ["Read(./.env)", "Read(./.env.*)"]}}`. The test rule uses a prefix match, so `npm run test` and `npm run test:unit` run freely, which keeps a TDD loop fast. Lint is allowed as an exact command. Push is in ask because it affects the shared remote and should always get a human check. The deny rules cover `.env` and variants like `.env.local`. Because deny beats allow, these stay blocked even if someone later adds broad read access. I commit this file so the team shares it. I avoid rules like `Bash(npm:*)`, which would also allow `npm install` of arbitrary packages.
keyPoints: Allow test (prefix) and lint commands for fast loops
Put `git push` under ask
Deny `.env` and `.env.*` reads
Deny beats allow, so secrets stay protected
Avoid overly broad prefixes like `Bash(npm:*)`

subjective.question: What are the ways to give Claude Code good context for a task, and when would you use each?
subjective.answer: First, @ mentions. Typing `@src/cart.ts` pulls the file into context, and an @ on a directory gives a listing. I use this when I know exactly which files matter, so Claude does not waste time searching. Second, images. I paste screenshots with Ctrl+V, even on macOS, or drag them in. This is ideal for UI bugs, design mockups or error dialogs. Third, issues. I paste the issue text or URL, or ask Claude to read it with the `gh` CLI if it is installed. This gives requirements and acceptance criteria in the author's own words. I can also pipe in logs or paste error output. Good context is specific: point to the relevant code, show the symptom and state the expected outcome, and avoid dumping whole folders.
keyPoints: @ file pulls content; @ directory gives a listing
Ctrl+V pastes screenshots, including on macOS
Link or paste issues; `gh` CLI can fetch them
Paste logs and error output
Be specific; do not flood context

subjective.question: Walk through a test-driven loop with Claude Code for a new feature.
subjective.answer: Step one: I tell Claude we are doing TDD and ask it to write tests from the expected inputs and outputs, with no implementation yet. Step two: I ask it to run the tests and confirm they fail for the right reason, not because of a typo or import error. Step three: I review the tests, because they are the specification, and then commit them. Step four: I ask Claude to write code that makes the tests pass without changing the tests. It runs the suite, reads failures and iterates. An allow rule like `Bash(npm run test:*)` keeps this loop fast. Step five: when all tests pass, I review the diff and check that the implementation is general, not hard-coded to the test cases. Then I commit.
keyPoints: Write tests first, no implementation
Confirm tests fail for the right reason
Review and commit the tests as the spec
Implement without modifying tests; iterate on failures
Check for overfitting, then review diff and commit

subjective.question: Why should you tell Claude not to modify the tests during the implementation step, and what other risks do you watch for?
subjective.answer: The tests are the contract. If Claude is allowed to change them, the easiest route to green is to weaken an assertion, skip a case or delete a failing test. Then the suite passes but the feature is wrong. Committing the tests first makes any change to them visible in the diff. I also watch for overfitting, where the code special-cases the exact test inputs instead of solving the general problem. Asking Claude to explain its approach, or adding one extra test it has not seen, exposes this. Other risks are mocking too much, so the tests no longer exercise real behaviour, and tests that pass on the first run, which means they never failed and may test nothing. Line-by-line diff review catches most of these.
keyPoints: Tests are the specification; editing them hides failures
Commit tests first so changes show in the diff
Watch for code hard-coded to test inputs
Watch for over-mocking and tests that never failed
Review the diff line by line

subjective.question: Explain the difference between `/clear`, `/compact` and `/context`, with an example of when you would use each.
subjective.answer: `/clear` wipes the conversation history and starts fresh in the same session. I use it between unrelated tasks, for example after finishing a login feature and before fixing a CSV bug, so old details do not distract Claude. `/compact` summarises the conversation to free space but keeps the important thread. I can add focus instructions, like `/compact keep the API design decisions and the failing test names`. I use it in a long session that is still about the same task. `/context` shows how the context window is being used, including how much space files, tools and messages take. I use it to decide whether I need to compact, or to spot something large, like a big file or many MCP tools, eating context.
keyPoints: `/clear`: fresh start between unrelated tasks
`/compact [focus]`: summarise a long, relevant session
Focus instructions control what the summary keeps
`/context`: view what is using the context window
Long, noisy context lowers output quality

subjective.question: How do you interrupt and rewind Claude Code when it goes in the wrong direction?
subjective.answer: If Claude starts doing something wrong, I press Esc. That stops the current action but keeps the session and context, so I can redirect it straight away, for example 'stop, the bug is in the parser, not the router'. Pressing Esc twice lets me go back to an earlier message, edit it and continue from there. This is useful when my original prompt was the problem. Claude Code also keeps checkpoints of its file edits, and the `/rewind` command can restore code or conversation to an earlier point. Checkpoints do not undo external side effects such as database changes or a push, so git is still my main safety net. The habit is to correct early. A two-second interrupt is cheaper than reviewing a long wrong diff.
keyPoints: Esc interrupts while keeping the session
Double Esc goes back to edit an earlier message
Checkpoints and `/rewind` restore earlier states
Rewind does not undo external side effects; use git
Correct course early

subjective.question: A colleague says 'permission prompts slow me down, I just run with `--dangerously-skip-permissions`.' How would you respond?
subjective.answer: I understand the frustration, but that flag turns on bypassPermissions, which means Claude can run any command with no checks. On a normal laptop that includes deleting files, pushing to remote, reading credentials, or acting on a prompt injection hidden in a web page or file. Reviewing the diff afterwards does not help, because commands have already run. If they really need it, for example for a long unattended migration, it should run only in an isolated container or VM with no sensitive access, no production credentials and limited network. For daily work, the better fix is a good allow-list: allow test, lint and build commands, use acceptEdits once the plan is approved, and keep deny rules for secrets. That removes most prompts while keeping safety.
keyPoints: The flag removes all permission checks
Risks: destructive commands, secret exposure, prompt injection
Only in isolated container or VM without sensitive access
Better: tuned allow-list plus acceptEdits
Keep deny rules for secrets

subjective.question: Describe how you would complete this week's task: use plan mode to add a feature with tests to a small app, and meet the checkpoint.
subjective.answer: I start a clean session with `/clear` and switch to plan mode. I describe the feature, @-mention the relevant files and paste any screenshot or issue text. Claude explores and proposes a plan. I check files, approach, tests and scope, and refine until I can predict the diff. After approval, I run a TDD loop: Claude writes failing tests, I confirm they fail for the right reason and commit them, then Claude implements without touching the tests. My project settings allow `npm run test:*` so the loop is fast, and deny `.env` reads. When tests pass, I run `git diff` and read every line: logic, edge cases, naming, no stray debug code, no unrelated changes. I ask Claude to explain anything unclear, run the full suite once more, then commit with a clear message.
keyPoints: Clean context, plan mode, @ mentions for relevant files
Review and refine the plan before approving
TDD: failing tests committed first, then implementation
Sensible allow and deny rules for a fast, safe loop
Line-by-line diff review and full test run before commit

subjective.question: You review this proposed project `.claude/settings.json` before it is committed. What is wrong with it, and how would you fix it?
subjective.answer: This file has four problems. First, `defaultMode: bypassPermissions` turns off every safety prompt for the whole team, and everyone who clones the repo inherits it. I would remove it, or set the mode to `plan` for larger work. Second, `Bash(*)` approves any shell command, including `rm -rf`, `curl` uploads and `git push --force`. I would replace it with narrow rules such as `Bash(npm run test:*)` and `Bash(npm run lint)`. Third, the deny list is empty. I would add `Read(./.env)`, `Read(./.env.*)` and `Read(./secrets/**)`, and put `Bash(git push:*)` under ask. Fourth, and worst, a live secret key sits in a committed file. It must be removed and the key rotated, because it may already be in git history. Secrets belong in a secrets manager or in local environment variables, never in shared settings.
keyPoints: bypassPermissions in shared settings removes safety for the whole team
`Bash(*)` is far too broad; use narrow command-prefix rules
Add deny rules for env and secret files, and an ask rule for push
Committed secrets must be removed and the key rotated

subjective.question: You approved a plan that changes three files. After Claude finishes, `git diff --stat` shows seven changed files. How do you handle this?
subjective.answer: First, I would not commit anything. I would run `git diff` and read every file that was not in the plan, so I know whether each change is necessary, such as a type update the plan missed, or just scope creep, like reformatting or an unrelated refactor. Then I would ask Claude to explain why it touched each extra file. If a change is unneeded, I either rewind to the checkpoint taken before the edits, or tell Claude to revert those specific files and keep only what the plan covered. If an extra file really is needed, I make sure tests cover it. Next time, I would add constraints to my prompt and plan, such as 'only modify these files; ask before touching anything else'. I would also stay in manual approval rather than acceptEdits, so each edit is visible as it happens. Only a diff I have reviewed line by line gets committed.
keyPoints: Do not commit until the unexpected files are reviewed
Ask Claude to justify each out-of-plan change
Revert unneeded changes by rewinding or targeted reverts
Constrain scope in the prompt and use manual edit approval

subjective.question: Your team is adopting Claude Code on a shared repository. How would you set up settings files and CLAUDE.md, so that team rules stay consistent while each developer keeps personal preferences?
subjective.answer: I would commit `.claude/settings.json` with the team baseline. It would allow safe, frequent commands like tests, lint and type-check. It would put `git push` and dependency installs under ask, and deny reads of `.env` and secret folders. I would also commit a CLAUDE.md covering the build and test commands, coding style, the package manager, and rules such as 'never edit generated files'. Each developer then uses `.claude/settings.local.json` for personal tweaks, such as allowing a command they trust on their own machine. Claude Code normally configures git to ignore this file, and I would check that it is ignored. Personal settings that apply across all projects go in `~/.claude/settings.json`. If the company needs rules nobody can override, such as blocking certain network commands, those go in enterprise managed settings, which have the highest precedence. Deny rules always win when rules conflict, so the safety rules hold whatever anyone adds locally.
keyPoints: Committed .claude/settings.json holds the team baseline
CLAUDE.md holds shared commands and conventions
settings.local.json (git-ignored) and user settings hold personal preferences
Managed settings enforce rules nobody can override; deny wins in conflicts

subjective.question: You need to implement a feature described in GitHub issue #142. How would you give Claude Code the context it needs before asking for a plan?
subjective.answer: I would start in plan mode so nothing is edited while Claude gathers context. For the issue itself, I would ask Claude to read it with the GitHub CLI, for example 'use `gh issue view 142` to read the issue and its comments', provided `gh` is installed and authenticated. If it is not, I would paste the key text directly into the prompt. If the issue includes screenshots, I would paste the image into the prompt with Ctrl+V. Then I would @-mention the files I know matter, such as the route handler and its existing tests, so Claude does not waste context searching. I would also point it at an existing feature to copy patterns from. Finally, I would state the constraints: acceptance criteria, which files are off limits, and that tests must be written first. With this context, the plan Claude produces is specific, and I can review it against the issue's requirements.
keyPoints: Work in plan mode while context is gathered
Read the issue via `gh` CLI or by pasting its text; paste screenshots too
@-mention the relevant files and an example pattern to follow
State acceptance criteria and constraints before asking for the plan

subjective.question: Three hours into a debugging session, Claude starts repeating fixes it already tried and forgetting constraints you gave earlier. Diagnose the problem and describe your recovery strategy.
subjective.answer: The likely cause is a long, cluttered context. Failed attempts, large logs and old file reads crowd out the important instructions, and auto-compaction may already have dropped details. I would first run `/context` to see how full the window is and what is using the space. If the session still holds valuable findings, I would run `/compact` with focus instructions, for example '/compact keep the root-cause hypotheses ruled out, the constraints, and the current failing test'. If the session is too muddled, a cleaner reset is better. I would ask Claude to write a short notes file covering what was tried, what was ruled out, and the next hypothesis. Then I would run `/clear` and start fresh with that file @-mentioned. Any rule that keeps getting forgotten should go into CLAUDE.md. To prevent this next time, I would avoid pasting huge logs and keep one task per session.
keyPoints: Symptoms point to a polluted or overflowing context
Use /context to inspect how much space is used and by what
Use /compact with focus instructions to keep key decisions
Or write a notes file, /clear, and restart with it; move durable rules to CLAUDE.md

subjective.question: You wrote this failing test before asking Claude to implement `applyCoupon`. Describe the prompts and checks you would use to take it from red to a reviewed green.
subjective.answer: First, I would ask Claude to run the tests and confirm they fail for the right reason. For example, `applyCoupon` is not exported or returns the wrong value, rather than there being a syntax error. I would commit the tests at this point. Next, I would prompt: 'Implement applyCoupon in cart.js so these tests pass. Do not modify cart.test.js. Do not special-case test inputs. Keep iterating until all tests pass.' While Claude works, I watch for edits to the test file, or a lookup that only covers these three inputs. Once the tests are green, I read the diff line by line. I check how coupon rules are stored, how rounding is handled, and the floor at zero. I would also add a test or two for other inputs, such as lowercase codes or a zero total, and confirm they still pass. Then I run the full suite and lint, and commit with a clear message.
keyPoints: Confirm tests fail for the right reason, then commit them
Explicitly forbid editing tests and special-casing inputs
Let Claude iterate to green, watching for test tampering
Review the diff line by line, add edge cases, run the full suite, commit

subjective.question: How do Claude Code checkpoints and rewind relate to git? Why should you still commit often during a plan-then-build task?
subjective.answer: Checkpoints are Claude Code's local undo history. Claude records the state before its file edits, and with Esc Esc or `/rewind` you can restore the code, the conversation, or both, to an earlier point. This is fast for undoing a wrong direction inside a session. But checkpoints have limits. They do not capture changes made by Bash commands, such as migrations, deleted files or installed packages. They do not cover edits you or other tools make outside Claude. And they are not a shared, permanent history. Git is the real safety net. I commit at each meaningful step: after the tests are written and failing, and again after each green step with a reviewed diff. That gives me points I can always return to with `git diff` or `git reset`, a clean history for reviewers, and small diffs that are easy to review line by line, which is exactly what this week's checkpoint requires.
keyPoints: Checkpoints restore Claude's file edits and/or conversation within a session
They do not undo Bash side effects or external edits
Git is the durable, shared history
Frequent small commits make line-by-line review and rollback easy

steps.overview: This step teaches you to customise Claude Code for a team. You will use custom slash commands for repeatable prompts, skills for packaged know-how that Claude loads when relevant, and hooks for deterministic automation such as auto-formatting and blocking edits to protected files. You will also learn which settings files to commit so every teammate gets the same behaviour. These topics appear in the Claude Code in Action course and in real-world team setups.
objectives: Create a project slash command in .claude/commands that accepts arguments with $ARGUMENTS.
Write a skill in .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md with a description that tells Claude when to load it.
Configure a PostToolUse hook that runs Prettier on every file Claude edits or writes.
Build a PreToolUse hook that uses exit code 2 to block edits to protected files.
Choose correctly between user, project and local settings files, and commit the right ones for the team.

concepts.explanation: A Markdown file whose body is a prompt template. Project commands live in .claude/commands/ and personal commands live in ~/.claude/commands/. The file name becomes the command, so review.md becomes /review. Subfolders help you organise commands, and /help lists the available ones.

$ARGUMENTS inserts everything typed after the command, and $1, $2 insert positional arguments. Optional YAML frontmatter can set description, argument-hint, allowed-tools and model. Inside a command, @path includes a file's contents and a line starting with ! runs a bash command whose output becomes context. A ! line needs a matching Bash entry in allowed-tools.

A skill is a folder containing SKILL.md, which has YAML frontmatter with name and description, plus optional scripts and reference files. At startup Claude reads only each skill's name and description. It loads the full content when the task matches that description; this is called progressive disclosure. Project skills live in .claude/skills/ and personal skills live in ~/.claude/skills/.

CLAUDE.md is always loaded, so use it for short, always-true project rules. A slash command runs when a human explicitly invokes it. A skill is loaded by Claude itself when relevant, so it suits longer, task-specific procedures that should not fill the context window all the time.

Hooks are shell commands that Claude Code runs automatically at lifecycle events. Unlike instructions in a prompt, they are deterministic: they always run. You configure them under the "hooks" key of a settings.json file, and you can view them with the /hooks command.

Key events are PreToolUse (before a tool runs, can block it), PostToolUse (after a tool succeeds), UserPromptSubmit, Notification, Stop, SubagentStop, PreCompact, SessionStart and SessionEnd. For tool events, a matcher selects tools by name, for example "Edit|Write"; a regex is allowed. An empty matcher or "*" matches all tools.

The hook receives JSON on stdin with fields such as session_id, tool_name and tool_input; tool_input.file_path holds the edited file. Exit 0 means success. Exit 2 is a blocking error: in PreToolUse it cancels the tool call and sends stderr to Claude. Any other non-zero code is a non-blocking error that is shown to the user.

~/.claude/settings.json holds user settings for all projects. .claude/settings.json holds project settings; commit it to share hooks and permissions. .claude/settings.local.json holds personal overrides and is gitignored. Enterprise managed settings take the highest precedence.

keyFacts: review.md in .claude/commands/ is invoked as /review; ~/.claude/commands/ holds personal commands that work in every project.
$ARGUMENTS inserts the full argument string; $1, $2 insert positional arguments.
SKILL.md frontmatter requires name and description. The description decides when Claude loads the skill, so state both what the skill does and when to use it.
Exit code 2 from a PreToolUse hook blocks the tool call, and stderr is sent to Claude as feedback.
A PostToolUse hook cannot undo the action, because the tool has already run. Use it for formatting, linting and logging.
Use the matcher "Edit|Write" to catch file changes. Match MultiEdit too if your version exposes that tool.
$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR points to the project root, so reference hook scripts with it rather than relative paths.
Hooks have a default timeout of 60 seconds per command, which can be configured per hook.
Commit .claude/settings.json, .claude/commands/ and .claude/skills/. Keep .claude/settings.local.json out of git.
Hooks run with your user's full permissions. Review every hook command before adding it, especially hooks that come from others.

example.caption: .claude/settings.json (committed): blocks edits to .env and lockfiles, then runs Prettier after every edit. Requires jq and Prettier in the project.

pitfalls: Putting the team hook in .claude/settings.local.json or ~/.claude/settings.json. It works for you but teammates never get it, so the checkpoint fails.
Using exit code 1 to block an edit. Only exit code 2 blocks; other non-zero codes are just reported to the user as errors.
Trying to block in PostToolUse. By then the file is already changed, so protection belongs in PreToolUse.
Writing a vague skill description such as "helpers". Claude decides whether to load a skill from its description, so a vague one means the skill is never loaded.
Running Prettier on every file type. Without --ignore-unknown, edits to unsupported files produce errors on every change.
Hard-coding relative script paths in hooks. They break when Claude's working directory changes, so use $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR.

workflow.title: Hands-on: Prettier hook plus shared /review command

steps.label: Install formatter and jq
steps.detail: Run npm install --save-dev prettier, and make sure jq is available on every developer machine.

steps.label: Add PostToolUse hook
steps.detail: In .claude/settings.json, add a PostToolUse entry with matcher "Edit|Write" that pipes tool_input.file_path into npx prettier --write.

steps.label: Add protected-file guard
steps.detail: Add a PreToolUse hook that exits with code 2 and writes a reason to stderr when the target path is .env or a lockfile.

steps.label: Create the /review command
steps.detail: Write .claude/commands/review.md with a description in its frontmatter and a prompt that asks Claude to review the changes for bugs, security issues, tests and style, focused on $ARGUMENTS.

steps.label: Verify with /hooks
steps.detail: Restart or reload Claude Code, open /hooks to confirm both hooks are registered, then ask Claude to edit a messy file and check it was formatted.

steps.label: Commit and share
steps.detail: Commit the .claude/settings.json and .claude/commands/ files, so teammates get the same hooks and /review after a git pull.

project.title: team-claude-setup
project.summary: A small repository that commits a shared Claude Code setup: a PostToolUse hook that runs Prettier after every Edit/Write, a PreToolUse hook that blocks edits to protected files, a `/review` slash command and a project skill. Teammates who clone the repo and run `npm install` get the same hooks, command and skill, because everything lives in `.claude/` and is checked into git.
project.run:
npm install
chmod +x .claude/hooks/*.mjs
claude
/hooks
> Create src/app.js with a badly formatted function
> Add a line to .env
/review src/

files.code:
---
description: Review uncommitted changes for bugs, security and style
argument-hint: [path or focus, e.g. src/ or "security"]
allowed-tools: Bash(git diff:*), Bash(git status:*), Read, Grep, Glob
---

You are reviewing my uncommitted changes before I open a pull request.

## Context

- Status: !`git status --short`
- Diff: !`git diff HEAD`

## Focus

The user asked to focus on: $ARGUMENTS
If that is empty, review all changed files.

## What to check

1. Bugs and edge cases (null values, wrong conditions, missing awaits).
2. Security: secrets in code, unsafe input handling, injection risks.
3. Error handling: follow the `api-errors` skill if HTTP handlers changed.
4. Tests: point out changed logic that has no test.

Do not comment on formatting. Prettier runs automatically after every edit.

## Output format

Reply with a table: File | Line | Severity (high/medium/low) | Issue | Fix.
End with a one-line verdict: "Ready to merge" or "Needs changes".
Do not edit any files. This command is read-only.

---
name: api-errors
description: Team standard for HTTP error responses in Node.js APIs. Use when writing or reviewing route handlers, middleware or error classes.
---

# API error handling standard

Claude loads this skill only when the task matches the description above.
The name and description are always visible; this body loads on demand.

## Rules

- Every error response uses this JSON shape:

```json
{ "error": { "code": "ORDER_NOT_FOUND", "message": "Order 42 not found" } }
```

- `code` is UPPER_SNAKE_CASE and stable. Clients depend on it.
- `message` is for humans. Never include stack traces or SQL.
- Use 400 for validation, 401 for no auth, 403 for no permission,
  404 for missing resources, 409 for conflicts, 500 for unexpected errors.
- Throw an `AppError(status, code, message)`; one central middleware
  turns it into the response. Do not call `res.status()` in many places.
- Log 500 errors with a request id. Do not log 4xx as errors.

## Checklist when reviewing

1. Does each new route have a 4xx path for bad input?
2. Is any raw `err.message` sent to the client?
3. Are async handlers wrapped so rejections reach the middleware?

# team-claude-setup

Shared Claude Code config for Step 4: commands, skills and hooks.

## What is inside

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `.claude/settings.json` | Shared, committed settings: permissions + hooks |
| `.claude/hooks/protect.mjs` | PreToolUse: exit 2 blocks edits to `.env`, lock file, `.git/`, hooks |
| `.claude/hooks/format.mjs` | PostToolUse: runs Prettier on `tool_input.file_path` |
| `.claude/commands/review.md` | `/review [focus]` slash command, uses `$ARGUMENTS` |
| `.claude/skills/api-errors/SKILL.md` | Skill Claude loads only when relevant |

## Try it

1. `npm install`, then start `claude` in this folder.
2. Run `/hooks` to confirm both hooks are registered.
3. Ask Claude to create a messy `src/app.js`. Open it: it is formatted.
4. Ask Claude to edit `.env`. The edit is blocked and Claude explains why.
5. Run `/review src/` to get a read-only review table.

## Command vs skill vs CLAUDE.md

- Command: you trigger it by typing `/review`.
- Skill: Claude decides to load it when the task matches its description.
- CLAUDE.md: always loaded; keep it short, project-wide facts only.

## Exit codes

- `0` success. `2` block (PreToolUse) or feed stderr to Claude (PostToolUse).
- Other codes: non-blocking error shown to the user.

## Settings hierarchy (highest wins)

1. Enterprise managed policy settings
2. Command-line arguments
3. `.claude/settings.local.json` (personal, git-ignored)
4. `.claude/settings.json` (this file, shared with the team)
5. `~/.claude/settings.json` (user, all projects)

Commit `.claude/settings.json`, `commands/`, `skills/` and `hooks/`.
Add `.claude/settings.local.json` to `.gitignore`.

revision.examFocus: This step maps to the customisation and automation part of the Claude Code in Action course: slash commands, skills, hooks and team settings. These are free completion courses, so expect short quiz questions and, later, interview questions. They test whether you pick the right mechanism (command, skill, CLAUDE.md or hook), the right hook event, the right exit code and the right settings file.

compare.difference: A command runs only when a human types /name. Claude loads a skill by itself when the task matches the skill's description.
compare.chooseA: Pick a command when the user should trigger a repeatable prompt on demand, such as /review or /fix-issue 123.
compare.chooseB: Pick a skill when Claude should apply packaged know-how automatically whenever it is relevant, such as a PDF-handling or house-style procedure.

compare.difference: CLAUDE.md is guidance the model reads and may not follow every time. A hook is a shell command the harness always runs on an event.
compare.chooseA: Use CLAUDE.md for conventions, architecture notes and preferences where judgement is fine.
compare.chooseB: Use a hook when the rule must hold every time with no exceptions, such as formatting after edits or blocking writes to .env.

compare.difference: PreToolUse runs before the tool and can stop it with exit code 2. PostToolUse runs after the change has already happened and can only react to it.
compare.chooseA: Choose PreToolUse to protect files, deny commands or check inputs before an action.
compare.chooseB: Choose PostToolUse to format, lint, run tests or log after an edit.

compare.difference: .claude/settings.json is committed and shared with the whole team. The local file is git-ignored and only for you in this repo. The user file applies only to you, across all projects.
compare.chooseA: Put team hooks, permissions and shared config in .claude/settings.json.
compare.chooseB: Put personal experiments and machine-specific tweaks in the local file, and your preferences for every project in the user file.

compare.difference: Only exit code 2 blocks the action and sends stderr back to Claude. Other non-zero codes are non-blocking errors shown to the user, and the tool still runs.
compare.chooseA: Use exit 2 when Claude must be stopped and told why so it can change course.
compare.chooseB: A script that exits 1 has failed but has not enforced anything, which is the wrong choice for protection.

cues.cue: must happen every time / deterministic / guaranteed
cues.why: Prompts and CLAUDE.md are followed most of the time, but only hooks are enforced by the harness.

cues.cue: prevent / block / protect a file before it changes
cues.pick: PreToolUse hook with matcher Edit|Write that exits 2
cues.why: Blocking only works before the tool runs, and only exit 2 blocks.

cues.cue: after every edit, format or lint
cues.why: The file exists by then and only needs tidying, not blocking.

cues.cue: team members should all get it / checked into the repo
cues.why: Only committed project files reach teammates through git.

cues.cue: Claude should use it automatically when relevant
cues.why: Skills are selected from their description. Commands need a human to type them.

cues.cue: pass an issue number or file name to a command
cues.why: Placeholders put user input into the saved prompt.

cues.cue: available in all my projects, just for me
cues.why: User-level locations apply everywhere but are never shared.

cues.cue: hook script not found when the directory changes
cues.why: An absolute path through the environment variable survives working-directory changes.

scenario.situation: Your team wants Claude Code to never modify files under config/secrets/. Every teammate must get this rule automatically after git pull. A developer has written a script that prints a message and exits with code 1, and placed it under PostToolUse in ~/.claude/settings.json. Which change makes the protection work for the whole team?
reasoning: Location: ~/.claude/settings.json is personal and never reaches teammates, so the config must move to .claude/settings.json and be committed.
Event: PostToolUse runs after the file has changed, so it cannot protect anything. The hook must move to PreToolUse.
Exit code: exit 1 is a non-blocking error, so the script must exit 2 and write the reason to stderr so Claude gets the feedback.
Matcher and path: match Edit|Write (plus MultiEdit if your version has it), read tool_input.file_path from the stdin JSON, and call the script through $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR.
scenario.answer: Add a PreToolUse hook with matcher Edit|Write in the committed .claude/settings.json. It runs "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR"/.claude/hooks/protect.sh, which exits 2 with a stderr message when the path is under config/secrets/. Only this combination blocks the edit and reaches every teammate.

memoryAids: PRE prevents, POST polishes: protection goes in PreToolUse, formatting goes in PostToolUse.
"Two stops you": only exit 2 blocks; 0 means OK, anything else just complains.
Shared = settings.json, Secret-to-me = settings.local.json: if it has 'local' in the name, it stays off git.
cheatSheet: Filename becomes the command: .claude/commands/review.md runs as /review. Subfolders help organise commands.
Command frontmatter can set description, argument-hint, allowed-tools and model. The body is the prompt.
$ARGUMENTS gives the whole argument string. $1, $2 give positional arguments.
A skill lives in .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md. Frontmatter needs name and description, and the description says what it does and when to use it.
Decision order: does a human trigger it? Use a command. Should Claude pick it up itself? Use a skill. Is it always-on context? Use CLAUDE.md. Must it be enforced? Use a hook.
A hook receives JSON on stdin (tool_name, tool_input such as file_path). Parse it with jq or a script.
Matchers are tool names or regex. Edit|Write catches file changes, and Bash catches shell commands.
The Prettier hook runs on PostToolUse with --write and --ignore-unknown, so non-supported files do not raise errors.
Exit 0 means success. Exit 2 blocks and feeds stderr to Claude. Any other code is a non-blocking error.
Default hook timeout is 60 seconds and can be set per hook. Keep hooks fast or every edit slows down.
Settings precedence: managed policy > command-line flags > .claude/settings.local.json > .claude/settings.json > ~/.claude/settings.json.
Hooks run with your full user permissions. Read every hook from others before enabling it, quote variables and avoid untrusted paths.
selfCheck: I can write a /review command that accepts arguments and explain where to put it for the team versus only for me.
I can write a SKILL.md whose description makes Claude load it at the right time, and explain why 'helpers' fails.
I can choose between command, skill, CLAUDE.md and hook for any requirement in one sentence.
I can configure a PostToolUse Prettier hook with matcher Edit|Write that reads file_path from stdin and uses $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR.
I can write a PreToolUse hook that blocks edits to protected files with exit 2 and a useful stderr message.
I can name which .claude files to commit and which to git-ignore, and state the settings precedence order.

objective.question: You save a file named review.md inside your repository's .claude/commands/ folder. How do teammates who pull the repo run it in Claude Code?
options: By typing @review
By running claude review in the shell
By typing /commands:review
By typing /review
objective.explanation: The file name without .md becomes the command name, so review.md is invoked as /review. The other forms are not how project commands are invoked.

objective.question: A developer wants a /standup command that works in every project on their laptop but is not shared with the team. Where should the Markdown file go?
options: ~/.claude/commands/
~/.claude/settings.json under a commands key
.claude/settings.local.json
.claude/commands/ in each repository
objective.explanation: ~/.claude/commands/ holds personal commands that are available in every project. Project .claude/commands/ is shared through git, and settings files do not hold command prompts.

objective.question: Your command file fix-issue.md contains 'Fix issue #$1 with priority $2.' A user types /fix-issue 482 high. What does Claude receive?
options: Fix issue #$1 with priority $2.
Fix issue #482 with priority high.
Fix issue #482 482 high with priority high.
Fix issue #482 high with priority .
objective.explanation: $1 and $2 are positional arguments, so 482 fills $1 and high fills $2. $ARGUMENTS would insert the whole string '482 high' instead.

objective.question: Which placeholder in a command file inserts everything the user typed after the command name, as one string?
options: $ALL
$ARGUMENTS
${input}
objective.explanation: $ARGUMENTS inserts the full argument string. $1 inserts only the first positional argument, and the other two are not Claude Code placeholders.

objective.question: You create .claude/skills/release-notes/SKILL.md. Which frontmatter fields are required?
options: description and model
title and trigger
name and allowed-tools
name and description

subjective.question: Explain what a custom slash command is in Claude Code and how you create one for your team.
subjective.answer: A custom slash command is a saved prompt stored as a Markdown file. When I type the command, Claude Code inserts that prompt as if I had written it. To create a team command, I add a file such as review.md to .claude/commands/ in the repository. The file name becomes the command, so this one runs as /review. The body holds the instructions, for example what to check in a code review and how to format the output. I can add optional frontmatter such as a description and an argument hint so it is clear in the command menu. Because the folder is committed to git, every teammate who pulls the repo gets the same /review. For commands that only I need across all projects, I put the file in ~/.claude/commands/ instead.

Project commands live in .claude/commands/ and are shared via git
File name becomes the command name, e.g. review.md → /review
Personal commands go in ~/.claude/commands/
Optional frontmatter like description improves discoverability

subjective.question: What is the difference between $ARGUMENTS and $1, $2 in a command file? Give an example of when you would use each.
subjective.answer: $ARGUMENTS inserts the whole string the user typed after the command name. $1, $2 and so on insert individual positional arguments split by spaces. I use $ARGUMENTS when the input is free text, for example /explain how the payment retry logic works, where I want the full question passed through. I use positional arguments when the command has distinct slots, for example /fix-issue 482 high with a prompt like 'Fix issue #$1. Treat it as $2 priority.' Positional arguments let me put each value in a specific place in the prompt and refer to it more than once. A useful habit is to add an argument-hint in the frontmatter, so teammates see what to type, such as the issue number followed by the priority.
keyPoints: $ARGUMENTS = entire argument string
$1, $2 = individual positional arguments
Free-text input suits $ARGUMENTS
Structured slots suit positional arguments
argument-hint frontmatter tells users what to pass

subjective.question: What is a Skill in Claude Code and how does Claude decide to use one?
subjective.answer: A skill is a packaged set of instructions, and optionally supporting files or scripts, that Claude loads only when it is relevant. It lives in a folder, for example .claude/skills/pdf-forms/, with a SKILL.md file at its root. SKILL.md has frontmatter with two required fields, name and description, followed by the detailed instructions. At the start, Claude only sees the name and description, not the full body. When a task matches the description, Claude loads the rest. So the description is the trigger. It must say both what the skill does and when to use it, for example 'Fills and validates PDF forms. Use when the user asks to fill, read or check a PDF form.' This keeps context small while still giving Claude deep, specialised guidance on demand.
keyPoints: Skill = folder with SKILL.md plus optional resources
Frontmatter requires name and description
Claude loads the full skill only when relevant
Description must state what it does and when to use it
Saves context compared with always-loaded instructions

subjective.question: Compare a slash command, a skill and CLAUDE.md. When would you choose each?
subjective.answer: CLAUDE.md is loaded into every session in that project. I use it for short, always-true facts: build and test commands, code style rules, folder layout and things Claude must never do. A slash command is triggered by a person. I use it for a workflow I want to start on purpose, such as /review or /release, where the human decides when it runs. A skill is triggered by Claude based on its description. I use it for specialised knowledge that is only needed for some tasks, like how we write database migrations or generate API clients. Putting that into CLAUDE.md would waste context in every session, and making it a command would rely on people remembering to run it. A simple rule: always needed goes in CLAUDE.md, user-started goes in a command, needed-sometimes goes in a skill.
keyPoints: CLAUDE.md: always loaded, short project facts
Command: user explicitly invokes it
Skill: Claude loads it when the description matches
Avoid bloating CLAUDE.md with situational detail
Choose based on who triggers it and how often it is needed

subjective.question: What are hooks in Claude Code, and why use a hook instead of just writing 'always run Prettier' in CLAUDE.md?
subjective.answer: Hooks are shell commands that Claude Code runs automatically at fixed points in its lifecycle, such as before or after a tool call, when a prompt is submitted, or when Claude finishes. They are configured in settings files. An instruction in CLAUDE.md is guidance: the model usually follows it, but it can forget, skip it under a long task, or decide it is not needed. A hook is deterministic. If I configure a PostToolUse hook to run Prettier on edited files, it runs every time, whatever the model decides. That is why rules that must always happen, like formatting, linting, logging or blocking protected files, belong in hooks. CLAUDE.md is still useful to explain why the rule exists, but enforcement should not depend on the model remembering.
keyPoints: Hooks are shell commands run at lifecycle events
Configured in settings.json
Deterministic, unlike prompt instructions
Use for must-happen actions: format, lint, log, block
CLAUDE.md explains; hooks enforce

subjective.question: Describe how you would configure a hook that runs Prettier after every file edit. Mention the event, matcher and how the hook gets the file path.
subjective.answer: I add a hooks section to .claude/settings.json under the PostToolUse event, because formatting must happen after the file is written. The matcher is "Edit|Write" so it fires for file-changing tools; if my version exposes MultiEdit, I add that too. The hook type is command. Claude Code sends JSON about the tool call on stdin, and for edits tool_input contains file_path. So the command reads stdin, extracts the path with jq, and runs npx prettier --write on that file. I would put this logic in a small script and reference it as "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR"/.claude/hooks/format.sh so it works from any working directory. The script should skip file types Prettier does not handle and exit 0 on success. Then I commit settings.json and the script so the whole team gets it.

Matcher "Edit|Write" (plus MultiEdit if available)
Read JSON on stdin, extract tool_input.file_path
Reference script via $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR
Commit settings.json and script for the team

subjective.question: How would you block Claude from editing protected files such as .env or files in a migrations folder?
subjective.answer: I use a PreToolUse hook, because it runs before the tool executes and can stop it. The matcher is "Edit|Write" so it catches file changes. The hook script reads the JSON from stdin, takes the file path from tool_input, and checks it against a list of protected patterns such as .env, secrets folders or applied migrations. If the path matches, the script writes a clear reason to stderr, for example 'Do not edit .env; ask the user to change secrets manually', and exits with code 2. Exit code 2 blocks the tool call, and the stderr text goes back to Claude, so it understands why and can choose another approach. If the path is fine, the script exits 0 and the edit goes ahead. A PostToolUse hook would be too late here.
keyPoints: Use PreToolUse, not PostToolUse
Match Edit|Write and read file path from stdin JSON
Exit code 2 blocks the call
stderr message is fed back to Claude
Exit 0 allows the edit

subjective.question: Explain hook exit codes: what do 0, 2 and other non-zero codes mean?
subjective.answer: Exit code 0 means success. The action continues normally. For most events stdout is shown in the transcript or verbose view rather than to the model, though some events like UserPromptSubmit and SessionStart can add stdout as context. Exit code 2 is a blocking error. What it blocks depends on the event: in PreToolUse it stops the tool call and sends stderr to Claude as feedback; in UserPromptSubmit it blocks the prompt; in Stop it prevents Claude from stopping. In PostToolUse the tool already ran, so exit 2 only sends stderr to Claude so it can react, it cannot undo anything. Any other non-zero exit code is a non-blocking error. Execution continues and the stderr is shown to the user, not used to block. So if I want to stop something, I must use exit 2 in the right event, not just any failure code.
keyPoints: 0 = success, continue
2 = blocking error, stderr to Claude
Effect of 2 depends on the event
PostToolUse cannot undo the action
Other non-zero = non-blocking, shown to user

subjective.question: Name the main hook events in Claude Code and give a practical use for three of them.
subjective.answer: The main events are PreToolUse and PostToolUse around tool calls, UserPromptSubmit when the user sends a prompt, Notification when Claude Code sends a notification such as needing permission, Stop when the main agent finishes, SubagentStop when a subagent finishes, PreCompact before context compaction, and SessionStart and SessionEnd. Practical uses: PreToolUse to block edits to protected files or risky Bash commands, returning exit 2 with a reason. PostToolUse to run Prettier or a linter on each edited file, or to log changes for audit. Stop to run a quick check, such as type checking, and if it fails, return exit 2 so Claude keeps working and fixes the errors. SessionStart is also handy for loading context like the current branch or open tickets. Matchers apply to tool events, so I can target only Edit|Write or only Bash.
keyPoints: PreToolUse / PostToolUse around tools
UserPromptSubmit, Notification, Stop, SubagentStop
PreCompact, SessionStart, SessionEnd
Concrete use per event
Matchers target specific tools

subjective.question: Why should hook scripts be referenced with $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR rather than relative paths?
subjective.answer: A hook command runs in Claude Code's current working directory, which may not be the repository root. If Claude has changed into a subfolder, or a teammate starts Claude from a different folder, a relative path like ./scripts/format.sh can fail to find the script. The hook then errors and formatting or protection silently stops working. $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR is set by Claude Code to the project root, so a command like "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR"/.claude/hooks/format.sh always points to the right file. Quoting the variable also protects against spaces in the path. It also avoids hard-coding my own absolute home path, which would break on every teammate's machine. This matters most for shared hooks in .claude/settings.json, because they must work for everyone who clones the repo.
keyPoints: Working directory may not be the project root
Relative paths can fail silently
$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR always points to the project root
Quote the variable to handle spaces
Avoid machine-specific absolute paths in shared config

subjective.question: Explain the Claude Code settings hierarchy and which files a team should commit.
subjective.answer: Claude Code reads settings from several levels. User settings in ~/.claude/settings.json apply to all my projects. Shared project settings in .claude/settings.json apply to everyone working in the repo. Local project settings in .claude/settings.local.json are my personal overrides for that repo. Command-line arguments apply to a single session, and enterprise managed policy settings sit at the top and cannot be overridden. More specific levels generally override broader ones, with managed policy winning over everything. For a team, I commit .claude/settings.json with shared hooks and permissions, .claude/commands/ for shared slash commands and .claude/skills/ for shared skills. I keep .claude/settings.local.json out of git, since it holds personal preferences and sometimes machine-specific values. Claude Code typically adds it to gitignore, but I still check.
keyPoints: User: ~/.claude/settings.json
Shared project: .claude/settings.json (commit)
Local project: .claude/settings.local.json (do not commit)
Enterprise managed policy has highest priority
Commit .claude/commands/ and .claude/skills/ too

subjective.question: What security risks do hooks introduce, and how should a team manage them?
subjective.answer: Hooks run shell commands automatically with my user's full permissions. There is no sandbox. A hook can read files, delete data, send secrets over the network or install software, and it runs without asking each time. If a hook arrives through a pull request, or I copy one from a blog, I am effectively agreeing to run that code on every matching event. So the team should treat hook changes like production code: review every command in .claude/settings.json and every script under .claude/hooks/ before merging, use CODEOWNERS on those paths, avoid piping remote scripts into bash, quote variables, validate inputs from the stdin JSON, and skip sensitive paths. Claude Code also asks you to review hook changes made outside the session before they take effect, which is a useful safety step.
keyPoints: Hooks run with full user permissions, no sandbox
They execute automatically on matching events
Review all hook commands and scripts, especially from others
Use code review/CODEOWNERS for .claude/ paths
Validate input, quote variables, avoid remote script execution

subjective.question: Write out what a good /review command file might contain, and explain your choices.
subjective.answer: I would create .claude/commands/review.md. Frontmatter would include a description like 'Review current changes for bugs, security and style' and an argument-hint for an optional focus area. The body would tell Claude to look at the current diff, for example staged and unstaged changes against the main branch, then check for correctness bugs, missing error handling, security issues like secrets or injection, test coverage, and our naming conventions. I would add 'Extra focus: $ARGUMENTS' so /review performance narrows the review. I would ask for output grouped by severity with file and line references, and tell it not to edit files, only report. If my version supports it, I can restrict allowed-tools to read-only git commands. Committing it means every teammate runs the same checklist, which makes reviews consistent.

Frontmatter: description and argument-hint
Clear checklist and scope (the diff)
$ARGUMENTS for optional focus
Structured output, read-only behaviour, committed to git

subjective.question: Your Prettier PostToolUse hook is configured, but files are not being formatted. How would you debug it?
subjective.answer: First I check the configuration is loaded: I run the /hooks command to see registered hooks, and confirm the hook is in .claude/settings.json under PostToolUse with matcher "Edit|Write". Matchers are case-sensitive, so 'edit' would not match. If my version uses MultiEdit, I add it to the matcher. Next, I start Claude Code with debug output to see whether the hook fires and what it returns. Then I test the script by hand: pipe a sample JSON with tool_input.file_path into it and check that jq extracts the path and Prettier runs. Common causes are a relative script path instead of $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR, a missing execute permission, jq or Prettier not installed, the hook timing out, or settings edited outside the session that still need review before they apply.

Run with debug output to see execution
Test the script manually with sample stdin JSON
Check paths, permissions, dependencies, timeout

subjective.question: A teammate wrote this PostToolUse hook script for Prettier. Review it. What can go wrong, and how would you fix it?
subjective.answer: The script has three main problems. First, $FILE is not quoted, so any path with spaces breaks into several arguments. Second, it runs Prettier on every file Claude touches, including Python or Go files. Prettier errors on those, and the non-zero exit shows up as a hook error after every edit. Third, it never checks for an empty or null file_path. I would quote "$FILE" and exit 0 early if it is empty or "null". I would filter by extension with a case statement, or pass --ignore-unknown. I would also use the local binary through npx --no-install, or the node_modules/.bin path, so it does not try a slow download. Finally, I would end with exit 0 so a formatting problem never looks like a blocking failure. I would reference the script with "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR" in settings.json and test it by piping sample JSON into it.
keyPoints: Quote the path variable
Skip unsupported file types (case statement or --ignore-unknown)
Handle an empty or null file_path
Avoid slow npx downloads and exit cleanly
Test by piping sample hook JSON to the script

subjective.question: Your team wants Claude to always know the current git branch and the open ticket ID when a session starts, without anyone typing it. How would you do this with hooks?
subjective.answer: I would add a SessionStart hook. For SessionStart, whatever the hook prints to stdout on exit 0 is added to Claude's context. The script would run git branch --show-current. It would extract the ticket ID from the branch name, for example feature/PROJ-123-login, and print a short line such as 'Current branch feature/PROJ-123-login, ticket PROJ-123.' I can use the matcher to choose when it runs: startup, resume, clear or compact. Including compact means the context comes back after compaction. The script must be fast and must not print noise, because every line costs context. For information that changes during a session, a UserPromptSubmit hook works the same way: its stdout is added as context for that prompt. Both approaches can also return JSON with additionalContext. I would commit the hook in .claude/settings.json so everyone gets it, and use $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR for the script path.
keyPoints: SessionStart stdout is added to Claude's context
Matchers: startup, resume, clear, compact
Keep the output short and the script fast
UserPromptSubmit can inject context for each prompt
Commit to shared project settings

subjective.question: Explain progressive disclosure in Skills. How would you structure a large 'api-design' skill with style rules, examples and a validation script?
subjective.answer: Progressive disclosure means Claude does not load everything up front. At session start, only each skill's name and description are in context. When a request matches the description, Claude reads the SKILL.md body. Extra files in the skill folder are read only when SKILL.md points to them and the task needs them. Scripts can be run so that only their output enters context, not their full source. For an api-design skill, I would write a clear description of what it covers and when to use it, for example 'Use when designing or changing REST endpoints'. SKILL.md would hold the core rules and short steps. I would move long material into separate files such as reference/naming.md and examples/pagination.md, each linked with a one-line note on when to read it. I would add scripts/validate_openapi.sh for Claude to run against the spec. This keeps context lean, lets the skill grow without slowing every session, and makes the deterministic checks reliable.
keyPoints: Only name and description load at start
SKILL.md body loads when the request matches
Supporting files load on demand when referenced
Scripts are executed, and only their output uses context
A specific description triggers the skill

subjective.question: Your lead asks you to make sure Claude never ends a task with failing lint. Design a solution with hooks and explain the risks.
subjective.answer: I would use a Stop hook, which runs when Claude is about to finish its response. The script runs the linter, ideally only on changed files so it stays fast. If lint fails, it writes the errors to stderr and exits with code 2. Claude Code then blocks the stop and gives that stderr to Claude, so Claude fixes the problems and tries again. The main risk is an endless loop when Claude cannot fix something, such as a broken rule or an environment issue. To prevent that, the script reads stop_hook_active from the JSON on stdin. If it is true, the script exits 0, or it allows only a limited number of retries. I would also set a sensible timeout and keep the output short. A PostToolUse lint hook can complement this by giving earlier feedback after each edit. I would commit the hook in .claude/settings.json and also enforce lint in CI, because hooks only cover Claude's sessions.
keyPoints: Stop hook with exit 2 sends stderr back to Claude
Guard against loops with stop_hook_active or a retry cap
Lint only changed files, and set a timeout
PostToolUse can give earlier feedback
Still enforce lint in CI
