---
description: Check that this portfolio meets the Step 8 checkpoint
allowed-tools: mcp__portfolio__portfolio_checklist, mcp__portfolio__list_certificates, Bash(git log:*)
---

You are reviewing my Claude Code portfolio repository.

1. Call the `portfolio_checklist` MCP tool. Report each item as OK or MISSING.
2. Call `list_certificates`. Flag any course whose URL is still a placeholder.
3. Run `git log --oneline -5`. Confirm the hooks, command and CI work is committed.
4. End with a short to-do list, ordered by priority. Do not edit any files.

Extra focus from the user (may be empty): $ARGUMENTS

# Claude in CI: mention @claude in an issue or PR comment to get help.
name: Claude Code

on:
  issue_comment:
    types: [created]
  pull_request_review_comment:
    types: [created]
  issues:
    types: [opened]

jobs:
  claude:
    # Run only when someone mentions @claude
    if: |
      (github.event_name == 'issue_comment' && contains(github.event.comment.body, '@claude')) ||
      (github.event_name == 'pull_request_review_comment' && contains(github.event.comment.body, '@claude')) ||
      (github.event_name == 'issues' && contains(github.event.issue.body, '@claude'))
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write       # let Claude push commits to a branch
      pull-requests: write  # let Claude comment on and open PRs
      issues: write
      id-token: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 1

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      # Lets the portfolio MCP server from .mcp.json run in CI too
      - run: pip install "mcp[cli]"

      - uses: anthropics/claude-code-action@v1
        with:
          anthropic_api_key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}  # repo secret, never hard-code
          claude_args: "--max-turns 10"

revision.examFocus: This step covers the end-of-course quizzes in Claude Code in Action and Introduction to Model Context Protocol, plus the optional Building with the Claude API course. The quizzes test practical choices more than memorised facts: which slash command to use, which hook event can block an action, which MCP primitive fits a need, and where config or secrets belong. Interviewers later test the same ideas against your portfolio repository.

compare.difference: /clear throws the whole conversation away. /compact keeps a summary so Claude remembers what it learned.
compare.chooseA: Pick /clear when you are switching to an unrelated task and the old context would only confuse Claude.
compare.chooseB: Pick /compact when you are continuing the same task but the context is getting long.

compare.difference: PreToolUse runs before the tool call and can block it with exit code 2. PostToolUse runs after the action has already happened, so it can only report or give feedback.
compare.chooseA: Pick PreToolUse to stop something, such as reading .env files or running a dangerous command.
compare.chooseB: Pick PostToolUse to react to a finished edit, such as running a formatter, type checker or tests and returning the errors to Claude.

compare.difference: A tool is an action the model decides to call. A resource is read-only data that the application chooses to attach to the context.
compare.chooseA: Pick a tool when Claude itself should decide when to act, for example to create a ticket or query an API.
compare.chooseB: Pick a resource when the app or user supplies data, for example a document picked through an @-mention.

compare.difference: The first file is committed and shared with the team. The local file is personal and is kept out of git.
compare.chooseA: Pick settings.json for team rules, such as shared hooks and permission rules every developer needs.
compare.chooseB: Pick settings.local.json for your own preferences or machine-specific overrides.

compare.difference: The CLI command registers a server, by default for your local use only. A committed .mcp.json shares the server with everyone who clones the repository.
compare.chooseA: Pick claude mcp add for a quick personal setup or to try out a server.
compare.chooseB: Pick .mcp.json when the whole team should get the same server, and reference secrets through environment variables.

cues.cue: prevent, block, deny, stop before it runs
cues.pick: A PreToolUse hook that exits with code 2
cues.why: Only a pre-execution hook can stop a tool call. Claude receives the hook's stderr message as feedback.

cues.cue: after every file edit, auto-format, run type check
cues.pick: A PostToolUse hook with a matcher on edit and write tools
cues.why: The action has already happened, so the hook reacts to it and returns feedback.

cues.cue: the model decides when to call it
cues.why: Tools are the model-controlled primitive.

cues.cue: user picks from a menu or runs it like a slash command
cues.why: Prompts are user-controlled templates for a workflow.

cues.cue: attach data or a document to context, read-only
cues.why: Resources are application-controlled data, not actions.

cues.cue: test or debug a server before connecting it
cues.why: It lets you call tools and read resources in isolation, so you can tell whether a bug is in the server or in the client setup.

cues.cue: a reusable team workflow that takes input
cues.pick: A Markdown file in .claude/commands/ that uses $ARGUMENTS
cues.why: The file name becomes the slash command, and committing the file shares it with the team.

cues.cue: Claude is going the wrong way mid-task
cues.why: Escape stops the current action without losing the session.

scenario.situation: Your team uses Claude Code on a repository that has a .env file with database passwords. The lead wants Claude never to read .env. She also wants every file Claude edits to be type-checked, with the errors shown back to Claude, and the setup must work for every developer who clones the repository. What should you configure?
reasoning: Never reading .env is a blocking requirement, so it must happen before the tool runs. That means a PreToolUse hook on the read tools that exits with code 2 when the path contains .env. A PostToolUse hook is wrong here because the file would already have been read.
Type-checking after an edit is a reaction to a finished action. That means a PostToolUse hook on the edit and write tools that runs the type checker and sends the errors back as feedback.
The setup must apply to every developer, so put both hooks in the committed .claude/settings.json. settings.local.json is personal and is not shared.
Reject any option that pastes credentials into the hook script or the settings file. Secrets stay in environment variables or CI secrets.
scenario.answer: Add a PreToolUse hook that blocks reads of .env by exiting with code 2, and a PostToolUse hook that type-checks edited files and returns the errors. Put both in the shared .claude/settings.json so every developer who clones the repository gets them.

memoryAids: MCP control is 'Model–App–User = Tools–Resources–Prompts'. Remember it as 'TRP: The Robot Picks tools, the App Reads resources, the Person Prompts.'
'Pre prevents, Post points out.' Only PreToolUse can block, with exit 2. PostToolUse can only give feedback.
'Shared in settings, self in local, secrets in neither.'
cheatSheet: These are certificates of completion from Anthropic Academy, not proctored certifications. Call them 'completed Anthropic's Claude Code in Action course'.
Take the courses in this order: Claude Code in Action, then Intro to MCP, then optionally Building with the Claude API.
Complete every required lesson, or the certificate will not unlock.
Run /init at the start of a project to create CLAUDE.md, and commit the file so the team shares the context.
Use /compact to keep the task going in shorter context. Use /clear to start fresh.
Custom commands live in .claude/commands/<name>.md, which gives you /name. $ARGUMENTS holds the text typed after the command.
Hook exit code 2 in PreToolUse blocks the call, and stderr goes to Claude. PostToolUse cannot undo an action.
MCP tools are chosen by the model, resources by the app, and prompts by the user.
Debug a server with the MCP Inspector first, then add it with claude mcp add or a committed .mcp.json.
In CI, keep ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in GitHub Actions secrets and reference it in the workflow. Never hard-code it.
On LinkedIn, add the certificate under Licenses & certifications, with Issuing organization set to Anthropic and the credential URL.
Your portfolio repository should show CLAUDE.md, .claude/commands, the hooks in settings.json, a .mcp.json with no secrets, and the CI workflow.
selfCheck: I can explain when to use /clear, /compact and Escape, with a real example of each.
I can write a custom slash command that uses $ARGUMENTS, and say who gets it when it is committed.
I can choose PreToolUse or PostToolUse for a requirement and explain what exit code 2 does.
I can classify any MCP capability as a tool, resource or prompt by asking who controls it.
I can show a public repository with hooks, commands and a CI workflow that contains no secrets.
I can describe my certificates accurately on LinkedIn and in an interview, without overstating them.

objective.question: A colleague says the Anthropic Academy courses on the Claude Code path give a proctored professional certification. What do the three courses actually award?
options: A free certificate of completion for each course
A paid digital badge that needs an annual renewal exam
No certificate, only a course progress report
A proctored, time-limited professional credential
objective.explanation: Claude Code in Action, Introduction to Model Context Protocol and Building with the Claude API are free and each awards a certificate of completion. They are not proctored, paid or renewable credentials.

objective.question: You have one week to finish this step. In which order should you take the courses?
options: Claude Code in Action, then Introduction to Model Context Protocol, then Building with the Claude API (optional)
Any order, because all three courses are mandatory and independent
Introduction to MCP, then Claude Code in Action, then Building with the Claude API
Building with the Claude API, then Claude Code in Action, then Introduction to MCP
objective.explanation: The recommended path is Claude Code in Action first, then Introduction to MCP, then the optional Building with the Claude API. MCP makes more sense once you already use Claude Code, and the API course covers the API side.

objective.question: You are two hours into a Claude Code session. Responses are slowing down and the context is full of old debugging output. You still want Claude to remember the decisions made so far. What should you run?
options: /init
Press Escape twice and restart the terminal
/compact
/clear
objective.explanation: /compact summarises the conversation, so key context is kept and token use drops. /clear wipes everything, /init creates CLAUDE.md, and restarting loses the session.

objective.question: Claude Code has started editing the wrong module. You want to stop it at once and redirect it, without losing the session. What do you do?
options: Press Escape
Run /compact
Close the terminal window
Run /clear
objective.explanation: Pressing Escape interrupts Claude mid-task, and you can then give a corrected instruction in the same session. /clear and /compact manage context; they do not stop a running task.

objective.question: You create the file .claude/commands/review.md containing 'Review the file $ARGUMENTS for security issues'. How does a teammate use it?
options: Run claude review.md src/auth.ts
Run /run review --args src/auth.ts
Run /review src/auth.ts
Run /commands review src/auth.ts
objective.explanation: The file name becomes the command name, so review.md gives /review. Text typed after the command replaces $ARGUMENTS in the file.

objective.question: You open Claude Code in a new repository and want a project memory file that gives Claude the build commands, structure and conventions in every future session. Which command creates it?
options: /compact
/setup
/init
/memory create
objective.explanation: /init analyses the codebase and creates CLAUDE.md, which Claude Code loads as project context. The other options either do something else or are not the standard command for this.

objective.question: In an MCP server you expose a 'summarise-incident' template. The user picks it from a menu in the client before anything is sent to the model. Which MCP primitive is this?
options: Prompt, because it is user-controlled
Sampling, because it is server-controlled
Resource, because it is application-controlled
Tool, because it is model-controlled
objective.explanation: Prompts are user-controlled templates that the user chooses to invoke. Tools are model-controlled and resources are application-controlled.

objective.question: Your MCP server exposes a read-only list of database table schemas. The client application decides when to fetch it and attach it as context; the model does not call it as an action. Which primitive fits best?
options: Resource
Hook
Prompt
Tool
objective.explanation: Resources are application-controlled data that the client decides to read and include. A tool would be chosen and called by the model, a prompt by the user, and hooks are a Claude Code feature, not an MCP primitive.

objective.question: You have written a new MCP server. Before connecting it to Claude Code, you want to list its tools and call them by hand to check inputs and outputs. What should you use?
options: A PostToolUse hook
The GitHub Actions log viewer
/compact inside Claude Code
The MCP Inspector
objective.explanation: The MCP Inspector is the tool for testing an MCP server directly: you can see and invoke its tools, resources and prompts. The other options do not test a server in isolation.

objective.question: Every developer on your team must get the same MCP server configuration when they clone the repository. What is the best approach?
options: Commit a project-level .mcp.json file to the repository
Put the server details in CLAUDE.md as plain text
Add the server only with a PostToolUse hook
Ask each developer to paste the config into their shell profile
objective.explanation: A project-level .mcp.json is checked into the repo, so everyone shares the same servers (it can be created with claude mcp add using project scope). CLAUDE.md is guidance text, not server config, and hooks do not register servers.

objective.question: You want Claude Code to never read or edit the .env file. A hook script checks the file path in the tool input. How should it stop the action?
options: Run as a PreToolUse hook and exit with code 2
Run as a PreToolUse hook and exit with code 0
Run as a PostToolUse hook and exit with code 1
Run as a PostToolUse hook and delete the changes
objective.explanation: A PreToolUse hook runs before the tool call, and exit code 2 blocks it; the stderr message is fed back to Claude. Exit code 0 allows the call, and PostToolUse runs too late to prevent it.

objective.question: A PostToolUse hook runs a type checker after every file edit and finds errors. What can this hook do?
options: Prevent the edit from being written to disk
Return feedback about the errors so Claude can fix them
Nothing, because PostToolUse hooks cannot send output to Claude
Undo the edit automatically by returning exit code 2
objective.explanation: A PostToolUse hook runs after the action has happened, so it cannot undo or prevent it. It can return feedback, for example the type errors, so Claude corrects the code in its next step.

objective.question: You are adding a GitHub Actions workflow that runs Claude on pull requests. Where should ANTHROPIC_API_KEY live?
options: In CLAUDE.md so Claude can find it
As a GitHub Actions repository secret referenced from the workflow
In a committed .env file at the repo root
In .github/workflows/claude.yml as a plain env value
objective.explanation: Store the key as a GitHub Actions secret and reference it as secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the workflow. Never commit the key to any file, because anyone with repo access, or the public if the repo is public, could use it.

objective.question: You finished Claude Code in Action and want to add the certificate to LinkedIn. Which steps are correct?
options: Add profile section > Education, School: Anthropic, upload a screenshot
Post it as a Featured link only, with no issuing organization
Add profile section > Licenses & certifications, Issuing organization: Skilljar, leave the URL blank
Add profile section > Licenses & certifications, Issuing organization: Anthropic, paste the credential URL
objective.explanation: The checkpoint uses Licenses & certifications, with Anthropic as the issuing organization and the credential URL so others can verify it. Education is for degrees, and leaving out the URL makes verification harder.

objective.question: A PreToolUse hook is configured as shown. Inside check_path.py, how does the script find out which file Claude is about to edit?
options: The script reads a JSON object from stdin and looks at tool_input.file_path
The script must parse the session transcript file to find the last tool call
The script reads the CLAUDE_TOOL_PATH environment variable
Claude Code passes the path as the first command-line argument ($1)
objective.explanation: Command hooks receive event data as JSON on stdin, including tool_name and tool_input. For Edit and Write, tool_input contains file_path. There is no positional argument or dedicated path environment variable, and parsing the transcript is unnecessary.

objective.question: A nightly cron job must ask Claude Code to summarise new TODO comments and pass the result to another script. No human will be at the terminal. Which invocation fits best?

code.code: claude -p "List new TODO comments added in the last 24 hours" --output-format json

options: It runs in print (headless) mode, answers once, prints machine-readable JSON, and exits
It only prints the system prompt and does not call the model
It creates a plan in plan mode and waits for approval before running
It starts an interactive session and waits for the user to press Enter
objective.explanation: -p (print) runs Claude Code non-interactively and exits after responding. --output-format json gives structured output that scripts can parse. The other options describe interactive mode or plan mode, which need a human.

objective.question: Your Claude API call returns the response below. What should your application do next?
options: Show 'Let me check the weather.' to the user and end the conversation
Resend the same request with tool_choice set to none
Run get_weather with the input yourself, then send a new request that includes the assistant turn and a user message with a tool_result block whose tool_use_id is toolu_01A
Nothing; Anthropic runs get_weather on its servers and will send the result
objective.explanation: Client tools are executed by your code. You append the assistant message and then a user message with a tool_result block that references the tool_use id. Claude then continues. Ending the conversation or disabling tools breaks the loop.

objective.question: A company wants one MCP server, hosted centrally, that hundreds of employees connect to from their own Claude Code installs over the network. Which transport should the server use?
options: stdio with the binary copied to every laptop
A shared .env file that contains the server's socket path
Streamable HTTP, served from a remote endpoint with proper authentication
stdio, because it is the default transport
objective.explanation: stdio runs the server as a local subprocess and suits single-machine tools. A shared remote server should use the HTTP-based transport (Streamable HTTP) with authentication. Copying binaries or sharing socket paths does not give a central, managed service.

objective.question: What is the effect of this .claude/settings.json?
options: The deny list is ignored whenever an allow rule exists
Claude must ask before every command listed in allow
Claude can run only npm and git; every other tool is disabled
Claude can run npm test scripts and git diff without asking; curl commands and reads under ./secrets are blocked
objective.explanation: Allow rules let matching tool calls run without a permission prompt. Deny rules block matching calls, and deny wins over allow. Tools that match neither list still work but prompt as normal; they are not disabled.

objective.question: You ask Claude Code to search a huge codebase for every place a deprecated API is used. The search output is large, and you do not want it to fill your main conversation. What is the best approach?
options: Delegate the search to a subagent, which works in its own context window and returns a summary
Turn off all tools so Claude answers from memory
Paste the whole codebase into CLAUDE.md
Run /clear before each search
objective.explanation: Subagents have a separate context window. Only their final result returns to the main thread, so the main context stays clean. /clear wipes useful history, CLAUDE.md is for concise project guidance, and disabling tools prevents the search entirely.

objective.question: This Claude API request fails with a validation error. What is the cause?
options: The Messages API has no 'system' role; the system prompt goes in the top-level system parameter
The first message must come from the assistant
content must always be a list, never a string
max_tokens must be at least 4096
objective.explanation: In the Messages API, messages use only the user and assistant roles. The system prompt is passed as the separate system parameter. A string content is valid, and there is no such minimum for max_tokens.

subjective.question: An interviewer asks: 'Are your Anthropic Academy certificates professional certifications?' How do you answer honestly and still make them count?
subjective.answer: I would say clearly that they are free certificates of completion from Anthropic Academy, not proctored credentials. They show that I finished Claude Code in Action and Introduction to Model Context Protocol, and passed the course quizzes. Then I would point to the proof that matters more: my repository. It has a CLAUDE.md made with /init, custom slash commands in .claude/commands, a PreToolUse hook that blocks edits to secret files, a PostToolUse hook that runs tests and gives feedback, a project .mcp.json, and a GitHub Actions workflow that runs Claude on pull requests with the API key stored as a secret. Being honest about what the certificate is builds trust. The working code shows I can actually use the tool.
keyPoints: Certificates of completion, free, not proctored
Do not overstate the credential
Back it up with a portfolio repository
Name concrete artefacts: commands, hooks, MCP config, CI

subjective.question: Why is the recommended order Claude Code in Action, then Introduction to MCP, then optionally Building with the Claude API?
subjective.answer: Claude Code in Action comes first because it teaches the daily workflow: prompting, CLAUDE.md, context control with /clear and /compact, custom commands, hooks and GitHub integration. Once you use Claude Code every day, MCP makes sense. You already know what a tool call is, and you can see why you would want to add your own tools, resources and prompts through a server. Introduction to MCP then teaches you how to build and test that server. Building with the Claude API is optional because it targets people writing their own applications. It covers the API side, like messages and tool use in code. That is useful for interviews and product work, but it is not needed to be productive in Claude Code. Each course builds on the one before it.
keyPoints: Claude Code in Action builds the daily workflow first
MCP extends Claude Code, so context from course one helps
API course is optional and for building your own apps
Each course builds on the previous one

subjective.question: What is CLAUDE.md, how do you create it, and what should a good one contain?
subjective.answer: CLAUDE.md is a Markdown memory file that Claude Code loads into context at the start of a session. Running /init makes Claude analyse the codebase and create a first version. I then edit it by hand. A good CLAUDE.md is short and practical. It lists the build, test and lint commands, explains the project structure and key modules, and states coding conventions such as naming, error handling and which libraries to prefer. It also records rules like 'do not edit generated files' or 'run tests before committing'. I commit the project CLAUDE.md so the whole team shares it, and I keep personal preferences out of it. I do not put secrets in it, because it is plain text in the repo and is sent to the model.
keyPoints: /init generates CLAUDE.md from the codebase
Loaded as project context each session
Commands, structure, conventions, rules
Keep it concise, committed, and free of secrets

subjective.question: Explain when you would use /clear, /compact and the Escape key during a Claude Code session.
subjective.answer: These three solve different problems. I press Escape when Claude is going the wrong way mid-task. It interrupts the work at once, and I can give a corrected instruction without losing the session. I use /compact when a long session on one task has filled the context with logs and old attempts. It summarises the conversation, so Claude keeps the important decisions but uses fewer tokens. I use /clear when I switch to an unrelated task. It wipes the conversation, so old context cannot confuse Claude or waste tokens. CLAUDE.md is still loaded after a clear, so project knowledge is not lost. A simple rule: Escape to stop, /compact to continue the same work, /clear to start fresh.
keyPoints: Escape interrupts mid-task
/compact summarises and keeps key context
/clear wipes conversation for a new task
CLAUDE.md still provides project context after /clear

subjective.question: Walk through creating a team-wide custom slash command that writes unit tests for a given file.
subjective.answer: I create a Markdown file at .claude/commands/write-tests.md in the repository. The file name becomes the command, so it is invoked as /write-tests. Inside I write the instruction, for example: 'Write unit tests for $ARGUMENTS using our test framework. Follow the patterns in the existing tests folder. Cover edge cases and error paths. Run the tests and fix failures.' $ARGUMENTS is replaced by whatever the user types after the command, so '/write-tests src/utils/date.ts' targets that file. I commit the file so every teammate gets the same command after a pull. Personal commands I do not want to share go in my user-level commands folder instead. I keep the prompt specific and point to existing conventions, so the output matches the codebase.
keyPoints: File in .claude/commands/ inside the repo
File name becomes the command name
$ARGUMENTS passes user input
Commit it to share with the team

subjective.question: Explain the three MCP server primitives and who controls each one, with an example.
subjective.answer: MCP servers expose three main primitives. Tools are model-controlled. The model decides when to call them, for example a 'create_ticket' tool that the model uses when the task needs a Jira ticket. Resources are application-controlled. They are data the client app chooses to read and add to context, such as a file, a database schema or a document. The model does not trigger them as actions. Prompts are user-controlled. They are reusable templates the user picks on purpose, such as a 'summarise this incident' template that appears in the client's menu. The control model guides design. If the model should act on its own, make it a tool. If the app should supply data, make it a resource. If a human should start a workflow, make it a prompt.
keyPoints: Tools: model-controlled actions
Resources: application-controlled data
Prompts: user-controlled templates
Use the control model to choose the right primitive

subjective.question: Describe your workflow from writing a new MCP server to using it safely in Claude Code across a team.
subjective.answer: First I build the server and define its tools, resources and prompts with clear names, descriptions and input schemas. Next I test it with the MCP Inspector. I connect, list each primitive, call the tools with good and bad inputs, and check the results and error messages. This catches bugs before Claude ever sees the server. Then I register it in Claude Code with claude mcp add. For a team I use project scope, which writes the config to a .mcp.json at the repo root, and I commit that file. Secrets such as tokens are not hard-coded; they come from environment variables on each machine. Finally I try it in a real Claude Code session and check that Claude picks the right tools for the task.
keyPoints: Design clear tool names, descriptions and schemas
Test with MCP Inspector first
Register with claude mcp add or a project .mcp.json
Commit .mcp.json; keep secrets in environment variables

subjective.question: Compare PreToolUse and PostToolUse hooks. Give one good use case for each.
subjective.answer: Both are shell commands that Claude Code runs automatically around tool calls, configured in settings and matched to tools such as Edit or Bash. A PreToolUse hook runs before the tool executes. It receives the tool name and input, and if it exits with code 2 the call is blocked and its stderr message is sent to Claude as the reason. A good use is blocking any read or edit of .env files or production config. A PostToolUse hook runs after the tool has finished. It cannot undo the action, because the change has already happened. It can return feedback that Claude reads, though. A good use is running the formatter or type checker after every edit and reporting errors, so Claude fixes them in the next step. So: Pre for guarding, Post for checking.
keyPoints: PreToolUse runs before the tool and can block with exit code 2
PostToolUse runs after and cannot undo
PostToolUse can return feedback to Claude
Pre for guardrails, Post for quality checks

subjective.question: Written exam: design a hook that stops Claude Code from reading or editing any .env file. Explain the configuration and the script logic.
subjective.answer: I add a PreToolUse hook in the project's .claude/settings.json. Its matcher targets the file tools, for example Read, Edit and Write, and its command runs a small script. Claude Code passes the hook a JSON payload on stdin that includes the tool name and tool input, including the file path. The script parses that JSON, takes the path, and checks whether it ends in .env or matches a pattern like .env.*. If it matches, the script writes a clear message to stderr, such as 'Access to .env files is blocked by project policy', and exits with code 2. That blocks the tool call, and Claude sees the message and changes its plan. For any other path the script exits with 0, so the call goes ahead. I commit the settings file and script so the rule applies to the whole team, then test it by asking Claude to open .env.
keyPoints: PreToolUse hook with a matcher on file tools
Script reads tool input JSON from stdin
Exit code 2 plus stderr message blocks and informs Claude
Exit 0 otherwise; commit and test it

subjective.question: How would you set up Claude to run in CI on GitHub, and what safety steps would you take?
subjective.answer: The simplest route is Anthropic's Claude Code GitHub Action. Running /install-github-app from Claude Code helps set up the GitHub app and the workflow. Otherwise I add a workflow file under .github/workflows by hand. The workflow triggers on events such as pull requests or comments that mention Claude. For safety, I store ANTHROPIC_API_KEY as a GitHub Actions repository secret and reference it from the workflow. I never write it in the YAML or commit it anywhere. I give the workflow the minimum permissions it needs, limit which tools Claude may use in CI, and keep a human review step before merging. The committed CLAUDE.md tells Claude the test and lint commands, so CI runs follow project rules. I also watch usage, because every run costs API tokens.
keyPoints: Use the Claude Code GitHub Action or a workflow file
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY as a GitHub Actions secret, never committed
Least-privilege permissions and restricted tools
Human review before merge; monitor cost

subjective.question: The checkpoint says your repository should show the hooks, commands and CI you built. What exactly would you put in that portfolio repository?
subjective.answer: I would make the repo easy for a reviewer to scan. At the root, a README explains what each part does and how to try it. A CLAUDE.md, first created with /init and then edited, holds the build commands and conventions. The .claude/commands folder has two or three useful custom commands that use $ARGUMENTS, such as /write-tests and /review. The .claude/settings.json defines hooks: a PreToolUse hook that blocks secret files with exit code 2, and a PostToolUse hook that runs lint or tests and returns feedback. A .mcp.json shows at least one MCP server, ideally a small one I wrote and tested with the Inspector. Under .github/workflows there is a workflow that runs Claude on pull requests using a secret for the API key. Finally, the README links to the certificates.
keyPoints: README explaining each artefact
CLAUDE.md and custom commands with $ARGUMENTS
Pre and Post hooks in settings
Project .mcp.json and a CI workflow using secrets

subjective.question: What does the optional Building with the Claude API course add, and when would you use the API directly instead of Claude Code?
subjective.answer: Building with the Claude API covers the developer side. You learn to call Claude from your own code with the Messages API, handle system prompts and multi-turn conversations, and use tool use, where you define tools and run them in your own application. It also covers working with features like streaming and prompt evaluation. I use Claude Code when I, as a developer, want an agent that works in my terminal or IDE on a codebase. I use the API when I am building a product feature for end users, such as a support assistant inside our app, or a batch job that classifies documents. In those cases I need full control over prompts, tools, cost and the user interface. Knowing both helps in interviews, because many teams use Claude Code for development and the API in production.
keyPoints: Course covers calling Claude from your own code
Messages API, system prompts, tool use
Claude Code for developer workflows on a codebase
API for product features and custom pipelines

subjective.question: You discover that ANTHROPIC_API_KEY was committed to a public repository last week. What do you do?
subjective.answer: I treat the key as compromised, even if I delete the file now, because it stays in git history and bots scan public repos fast. First, I revoke or delete the key in the Anthropic Console and create a new one. Second, I store the new key only as a GitHub Actions secret and in local environment variables, and I update the workflow to read it from secrets. Third, I check usage in the console for unexpected activity during the exposure window. Fourth, I remove the key from history with a history-rewriting tool if needed, and I tell the team to re-clone. Finally, I add prevention: .env in .gitignore, a secret-scanning check, and perhaps a PreToolUse hook that blocks Claude from writing keys into tracked files.
keyPoints: Treat as compromised; revoke and rotate immediately
Store new key as GitHub Actions secret and env variable
Review usage for misuse
Clean history and add prevention like .gitignore and scanning

subjective.question: Hooks and settings can live at user level, project level or local project level. How do you decide where a hook belongs and what to commit?
subjective.answer: I decide by asking who the rule is for. Rules that protect the project and should apply to everyone go in the project's .claude/settings.json, which I commit. Examples are blocking .env edits with a PreToolUse hook and running the test suite in a PostToolUse hook. Personal preferences that only make sense on my machine go in my user settings in my home directory, such as a desktop notification when Claude finishes. Machine-specific or experimental project settings go in .claude/settings.local.json, which is meant to stay out of git. I keep committed hooks portable: relative paths, scripts stored in the repo, and no secrets in the commands. Because hooks run shell commands automatically, I review hook changes in pull requests like any other code.
keyPoints: Project settings.json for team rules, committed
User settings for personal preferences
settings.local.json for local, uncommitted overrides
Keep hooks portable, secret-free and reviewed

subjective.question: You added a PreToolUse hook to .claude/settings.json, but it never seems to run when Claude edits files. Describe how you would troubleshoot it.
subjective.answer: First, I confirm Claude Code actually loaded the hook. I run /hooks to see the registered hooks, and I restart the session, because hook configuration is read when a session starts. Next, I check the JSON is valid and in the right file. It should be project .claude/settings.json, not a misspelled path. Then I check the matcher. Matchers are case-sensitive and match tool names such as Edit, Write or Bash, so 'edit' will not match. After that, I run the command by hand from the project root. I pipe in sample JSON on stdin to make sure the script exists, is executable, and uses the right relative path. Finally, I use claude --debug to see hook execution logs. I also check exit codes: only exit code 2 blocks the action and sends stderr back to Claude.
keyPoints: Verify with /hooks and restart the session
Valid JSON in the correct settings file
Matcher is case-sensitive and must match the real tool names
Test the script by hand with sample stdin JSON; check paths and permissions
Use --debug and check exit-code behaviour

subjective.question: Explain what this script does and what you would change before running it unattended on a shared build server.

code.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
claude -p "Fix all ESLint errors in src/" \
  --dangerously-skip-permissions \
  --output-format json > result.json

subjective.answer: The script runs Claude Code in headless print mode. It asks Claude to fix ESLint errors in src/ and writes the structured JSON result to result.json. The risky part is --dangerously-skip-permissions. It bypasses every permission prompt, so Claude could run any shell command or edit any file on a shared machine. I would remove that flag. Instead, I would grant only what the job needs with --allowedTools, for example Read, Edit and Bash(npx eslint:*), and I would add deny rules for network commands and secret paths. I would run the job inside a container or a disposable checkout, never on a long-lived box with credentials. I would give the job its own API key from the secret store, check the exit status and parse result.json, and open the changes as a pull request for human review, not push to main.
keyPoints: Identifies -p headless mode and JSON output
Explains the danger of skipping permissions
Replaces it with a scoped --allowedTools list and deny rules
Sandbox or container plus secret handling
Human review through a pull request

subjective.question: Using the Claude API, explain the full tool-use loop for a 'get_order_status' tool, from defining the tool to getting the final answer.
subjective.answer: First, I define the tool in the tools parameter: a name, a clear description, and an input_schema written in JSON Schema, for example an order_id string. I send the user message along with the tools. If Claude decides it needs the tool, the response has stop_reason 'tool_use' and a tool_use content block with an id, the name and the input. My code validates the input, calls my own order service, and builds a tool_result block with the matching tool_use_id and the result content. If the call fails, I set is_error. I then send a new request with the full history: the original user message, the assistant message containing the tool_use block, and a user message containing the tool_result. Claude may call more tools, so I loop until stop_reason is 'end_turn'. I also cap the number of iterations to avoid runaway loops.
keyPoints: Tool definition with name, description and input_schema
stop_reason tool_use and the tool_use block with id
Client executes the tool and returns tool_result with tool_use_id
Resend the full history and loop until end_turn
Error handling and an iteration cap

subjective.question: Design a project subagent that reviews code for security issues but must never modify files. Show the file and explain each part.

code.code:
---
name: security-reviewer
description: Reviews changed code for security issues. Use proactively after edits to auth, input handling or SQL.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
---
You are a senior application security reviewer.
Focus on injection, auth flaws, secrets in code and unsafe deserialisation.
Report findings as: file, line, severity, fix. Do not edit files.

subjective.answer: I save this file as .claude/agents/security-reviewer.md and commit it, so the whole team gets the subagent. The YAML frontmatter defines it. name is the identifier. description tells the main Claude when to delegate; words like 'use proactively' and concrete triggers make automatic delegation more likely. tools limits the subagent to Read, Grep and Glob. With no Edit, Write or Bash, it physically cannot change files, which is stronger than only saying 'do not edit' in the prompt. The body is the subagent's system prompt. It sets the role, the focus areas and a fixed output format, so the results are easy to act on. The subagent runs in its own context window, so a long review does not fill the main conversation; only the findings come back. I can also create and manage it with the /agents command.
keyPoints: Location .claude/agents/ and committed for the team
Frontmatter: name, description, tools
Tool restriction enforces read-only, stronger than prompt text
Body is the system prompt with a clear output format
Separate context window keeps the main thread clean

subjective.question: Your team is choosing between a stdio MCP server and a remote Streamable HTTP MCP server for an internal Jira integration. Compare them and recommend one, including security points.
subjective.answer: With a stdio server, the client starts the server as a local subprocess and talks over stdin and stdout. It is simple, needs no network setup, and suits personal or local tools. But every developer must install it, keep it updated, and hold their own Jira token on their laptop. A remote Streamable HTTP server runs once, centrally. Clients connect over HTTP, so updates happen in one place, and access can go through proper authentication such as OAuth, with audit logs. For a team-wide Jira integration, I would recommend the remote server. Security steps: require authentication and HTTPS, give the server's Jira credentials least privilege, validate all tool inputs, and log calls. Developers should still review tool calls in Claude Code, because tool outputs can carry prompt injection from ticket text. For quick local prototyping, stdio is fine.
keyPoints: stdio = local subprocess, simple, per-machine install and credentials
Streamable HTTP = central, remote, easier updates and auth
Recommendation justified for a team use case
Auth, HTTPS, least-privilege credentials, input validation
Prompt-injection risk from tool outputs

subjective.question: You must migrate a 40-file module from callbacks to async/await with Claude Code. Describe a safe workflow that keeps you in control.
subjective.answer: I start on a fresh git branch with a clean working tree, so every change is easy to review or revert. I switch to plan mode with Shift+Tab. Claude then reads the code and proposes a plan without editing anything. I ask it to think hard about ordering, shared helpers and tests, and I correct the plan before approving. I make sure CLAUDE.md lists the test and lint commands, so Claude verifies its own work. I split the migration into batches, for example one folder at a time. After each batch, Claude runs the tests, I review the diff, and I commit. A PostToolUse hook that runs the linter or type checker gives fast feedback. If Claude drifts, I press Escape and redirect it. Between batches, I use /compact to keep the context focused. Finally, I open a pull request so CI and a human review the whole change.
keyPoints: Clean git branch and frequent commits
Plan mode before any edits; review the plan
Small batches with tests run after each
Hooks or CLAUDE.md commands for automatic verification
Escape to redirect, /compact between batches, PR review at the end

subjective.question: You installed Claude's GitHub integration, but commenting '@claude fix this' on a pull request does nothing. What do you check?

code.code:
on:
  issue_comment:
    types: [created]
jobs:
  claude:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
      pull-requests: write
      issues: write
    steps:
      - uses: anthropics/claude-code-action@v1
        with:
          anthropic_api_key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}

subjective.answer: First, I check the Actions tab to see whether the workflow ran at all. If it did not run, I confirm the workflow file is on the default branch, because issue_comment workflows run from the default branch. I also check the trigger covers the event; review comments on code lines need pull_request_review_comment as well. If it ran but failed, I read the logs. Common causes are a missing or misnamed ANTHROPIC_API_KEY repository secret, or a revoked key. Next, I confirm the Claude GitHub app is installed on this repository; /install-github-app in Claude Code sets up the app and the secret. Then I check the job permissions: contents, pull-requests and issues need write access to push commits and post comments. Finally, I check organisation policies that restrict Actions or third-party apps, and whether the commenter has the access the action requires.
keyPoints: Check whether the workflow triggered at all in the Actions tab
Workflow on default branch; correct trigger events
API key secret exists and is valid
GitHub app installed; write permissions set
Org policies and commenter access
